title: BYD launches the new Tang EV, a luxury 5-seat SUV with two +30" screens for under $30,000
content:
Peter Johnson
| Nov 24 2026 - 7:40 am PT
launched the third-generation Tang, a large, high-tech five-seat flagship electric SUV, starting at under $30,000 in China.
BYD third-gen Tang EV prices and specs
The new third-gen Tang is positioned below the Great Tang, or “Da Tang” as it’s called in China, BYD’s larger seven-seat flagship SUV in its Dynasty lineup.
BYD held a launch event for its new flagship five-seat electric SUV on Tuesday. The third-gen Tang is available in three variants: standard Premium, Laser Premium, and Laser Flagship.
All versions come standard with rear-wheel drive (RWD), but buyers can upgrade the Laser Flagship model with an optional all-wheel-drive (AWD) steer-by-wire package for an extra 20,000 yuan ($3,000).
Prices for the standard Tang Premium start at 187,900 yuan, or about $28,000, significantly lower than its
pre-sale price
of 225,000 yuan ($34,000).
The Laser Premium and Laser Flagship models start at 207,900 yuan and 219,900 yuan, respectively, also well below the pre-sale price.
All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade LFP Batteries. RWD models use a single 402 hp (300kW) electric motor, delivering CLTC ranges of 453 miles (730 km) for the base Premium model and 528 miles (850 km) for the Laser Premium and Laser Flagship versions.
Upgrading to the dual-motor AWD powertrain bumps power to 690 hp (515 kW) and delivers a CLTC range of up to 478 miles (770 km).
The optional AWD steer-by-wire package adds a premium touch with a drive-by-wire digital chassis, reclining driver’s seats, a 35.4″ integrated Star Ring display screen, and intelligent electric all-wheel-drive.
BYD third-generation Tang EV interior (Source: Lu Tian)
All versions feature BYD’s Flash Charging tech, enabling it to charge from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes for a full recharge (10% to 97%).
Inside, the flagship SUV adopts a five-seat layout and is packed with huge digital screens and premium extras.
The third-gen Tang features two giant screens: a 35.4″ integrated Star Ring display and a 30″ panoramic theater screen.
BYD third-generation Tang electric SUV interior (Source: Lu Tian)
BYD said the five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers, claiming the new Tang SUV has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L. It also offers a generous 1,000 mm of legroom for rear passengers.
The flagship electric SUV is equipped with BYD’s latest tech and other features, including its God’s Eye B laser-assisted driving system with DiPilot300 and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.
BYD’s God’s Eye B uses a roof-mounted LiDAR to support ADAS features such as city navigation assist, high-speed navigation assist, and all-scenario parking assist.
The third-gen Tang also has BYD’s new high-speed tire blowout stability system, which can keep the vehicle stable and in its lane at up to 112 mph (180 km/h).
Measuring 5,045 mm long, 1,980 mm wide, and 1,760 mm tall, with a 2,950 mm wheelbase, BYD’s new Tang SUV is about the size of a Tesla Model X or BMW iX.
The third-gen Tang will join the larger Great Tang as BYD expands its flagship SUV lineup. The Great Tang received
over 150,000 preorders
Since it launched, BYD has sold over 10,000 Great Tangs a month for four consecutive months. Will the smaller five-seat Tang draw the same demand? Let us know what you think of it in the comments below.

title: Nuro pulls safety drivers from Lucid Gravity Uber robotaxis in Bay Area
content:
Robotaxi
autonomous driving
Lucid Gravity
Fred Lambert
| Nov 24 2026 - 7:32 am PT
Nuro is now testing Lucid Gravity robotaxis on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with nobody in the driver’s seat. The driverless testing starts in four Peninsula and South Bay cities, with a fleet of more than 100 Gravity SUVs delivered by Lucid for the program.
It’s the biggest step yet for the Uber-Nuro-Lucid partnership. But it comes with a quieter update: the public launch, originally promised for 2026, is now expected in Q1 2027.
Driverless in four cities, employee rides next
According to
Nuro’s announcement
, driverless testing covers Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale, with more Bay Area cities to follow next year. Uber employees will “soon” be able to ride in the driverless vehicles.
Nuro has run the Gravity robotaxis around the clock in the Bay Area and Houston since December 2025, but always with a safety driver. Before pulling the driver, the company says it ran no-vehicle-operator testing at its Las Vegas closed course, covering things like pedestrian encounters and right-of-way violations, plus large-scale simulation.
Tilo Schwarz, Nuro’s head of the Nuro Driver, pointed out that driverless operation “isn’t new” for the company. That’s fair. Nuro has run driverless delivery pods in California since 2020. But this is its first time doing it with a passenger vehicle.
The regulatory pieces were already in place. As
we reported in May
, the California DMV extended Nuro’s driverless testing permit to the Lucid Gravity, and the CPUC followed with a drivered pilot permit for carrying passengers.
A short list, and Tesla isn’t on it
Nuro says it’s one of just six companies allowed to test without a driver on California roads. The DMV’s list, last updated November 5, confirms it: AutoMo, Nuro, Tensor, Waymo, WeRide, and Zoox.
Tesla isn’t one of them. Its “Tesla Robotaxi LLC” entity only holds a permit to test with a driver in California, and it has no deployment permit either.
Waymo, of course, is the benchmark. It already runs a paid, fully driverless service across much of the Bay Area, including the Peninsula and South Bay where Nuro is just now pulling its safety drivers.
The timeline keeps sliding
When Lucid, Nuro, and Uber
announced the program in July 2025
, the plan was to launch “later next year” in a major US city. As recently as June, when Uber
named Houston as the second market
for mid-2027, the Bay Area launch was still slated for this year.
Now it’s Q1 2027. Not a huge slip, but it’s a slip.
The scale ambition has gone the other way. Uber’s purchase commitment grew from 20,000 vehicles to at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles with the Nuro Driver, starting with the Gravity and later Lucid’s upcoming midsize models. Uber will own and operate the cars with fleet partners, and they’ll only be available through the Uber app.
For context, Lucid delivered 3,806 vehicles in Q3 2026. At that pace, 35,000 robotaxis would take more than two years of Lucid’s entire output.
Electrek’s Take
This is real progress, and it deserves credit. Nuro got the permits, built a formal safety case, tested at a closed course, and only then took the driver out. That’s how it should be done, and it should be applauded, especially as some companies claim to lead in autonomy while being too chicken to get a permit in California.
But let’s keep it in perspective. Driverless testing in four suburban cities with a 100-car fleet is where Waymo was years ago. Waymo is already doing hundreds of thousands of paid rides a week, including in the same part of the Bay Area. Nuro and Uber aren’t catching up to Waymo in 2027.
The bigger question for me is Lucid. The partnership gives Lucid exactly the kind of volume it needs, and 35,000 vehicles is a big number for a company delivering under 4,000 cars a quarter.
If this program is successful, and that’s a big if, then it could really help Lucid get to its more affordable vehicle.

title: Tesla (TSLA), SpaceX race for year-end merger deal before new Congress
content:
Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX are working toward a year-end deadline to agree on their all-stock merger, according to the Financial Times. A signed deal by December 31 would land days before the new Congress, where Democrats have promised to dig into Musk’s companies, is sworn in on January 3.
The FT also named the directors negotiating for each side. Two of Tesla’s three are the same people who designed Musk’s $1 trillion pay package.
We’ve been tracking the Tesla-SpaceX merger since Musk first floated it in May, when we called it Musk’s fourth billion-dollar self-deal, and his first trillion-dollar self-deal. Earlier this month, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX could announce the deal as soon as December. The FT report adds a deadline, names and a vote threshold.
A year-end deadline, and January 3
According to the FT, the talks are “moving towards a potential year-end deadline,” even though people familiar with the negotiations say an agreement isn’t close. The combined group would be worth about $3.5 trillion, by far the largest merger ever.
So why year-end? Look at the calendar.
The new Congress is seated on January 3. As of November 24, AP’s count has Democrats at 258 House seats and 56 Senate seats. Democrats haven’t been subtle about what comes next: Sen. Ruben Gallego tagged Musk on X with “See you in January,” and SpaceX’s military contracts and Musk’s Starlink decisions over Ukraine are expected to be early investigation targets.
It’s not only Washington. Texas’ incoming attorney general told Bloomberg that a merger of this size “warrants tremendous scrutiny,” and Bloomberg had previously reported that the companies want to close before President Trump leaves office.
Who’s at the table
Tesla’s special committee is chair Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Jack Hartung, advised by Evercore. SpaceX is represented by Roelof Botha and Randy Glein, with Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs as advisers. Both banks also helped take SpaceX public in June.
Denholm and Wilson-Thompson should sound familiar. They were the two-person special committee that built Musk’s new CEO pay package after a Delaware judge voided his 2018 award. And that 2025 award has change-in-control terms that drop its operational milestones and vest earned shares at the deal price, so the committee that wrote it is now negotiating the deal that could trigger it.
Ira Ehrenpreis, a long-time friend of Musk, who chairs Tesla’s compensation and governance committees and has sat on SpaceX’s board since February, isn’t on Tesla’s committee, per the FT.
If you can believe it, Musk isn’t formally in the room. The FT says Texas governance rules keep him out of active negotiations, but both committees can consult senior executives for information. Every one of those executives reports to Musk.
The vote math
Any agreement goes to a separate extraordinary Tesla shareholder meeting, and it needs more than 50% of all outstanding votes, not just of votes cast. Abstentions and uncast shares effectively count as “no.”
That sounds like a high bar. But Musk holds about 20% of Tesla’s voting power, and nothing in the report says his shares will be excluded. If they count, he’s 40% of the way to approval before a single other shareholder votes. On the other side, Musk controls about 84% of SpaceX’s votes, so there’s no real suspense there.
Uncast retail votes are exactly what Tesla’s new auto-vote program, rolled out in its October proxy, was designed to reduce.
Then there’s the regulatory side. The FT says the deal could draw scrutiny in the US, China, Europe and the UK, with Tesla’s China operations sitting awkwardly next to SpaceX’s rocket and Starlink business, which does a lot of work for the US military. Giga Shanghai builds more than half of Tesla’s cars.
Electrek’s Take
Congress can’t block this merger. Antitrust review sits with Trump’s DOJ and FTC until 2029, plus China, the EU and the UK.
Top comment by kbrannen
It's probably already too late to escape Jan 3. The DoJ investigation into the merger will take a minimum of a few months. At the very least it looks like there is a 30 mandatory waiting period, so if the merger isn't announced by Dec 4, that 30 days takes them to Jan 3. That gives them 10 calendar days to finish negotiations and get stock holder approval and they have to give time for the voters to get their votes in. So short of some miracle, Musk isn't going to get this done before Jan 3 ... at least from my understanding and counting.
What congressional committees can do is subpoena. Committee minutes, the Evercore fairness work, emails between Denholm’s committee and Musk’s executives about how the exchange ratio got set. That’s the kind of record that got Musk’s 2018 pay package voided by a Delaware judge, and it’s the kind of record nobody wants dragged into a hearing mid-negotiation.
The talks are “not close,” yet there’s a deadline. When the deadline comes from the political calendar instead of the negotiation, the side that wants to close fast is the one giving ground. But in this case, Musk is both sides, but he is mainly SpaceX.
We’ve said it before, and we’ll keep saying it: the only vote that means anything here is a majority of Tesla shareholders not named Musk. Denholm, who is up for re-election at next week’s December 3 annual meeting, could commit to that today, but in her entire tenure as Tesla chair, she always did exactly what Musk wanted.

content:
Markets & Policy
A forthcoming French decree could require RG5 hail-resistant modules and qualified installation for residential PV systems up to 9 kW to qualify for the reduced 5.5% value-added tax (VAT) rate.
François Puthod
24 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
France is preparing to introduce stricter technical and installation requirements for residential solar systems seeking the reduced 5.5% VAT rate, including RG5 hail-resistance certification for modules and installation by a qualified professional, according to the National Federation of Solar Energy (FNES).
The new decree, which is expected to be published shortly, would introduce RG5 as a requirement for photovoltaic installations eligible for the reduced tax rate.
RG5 is the highest level of hail resistance in the European classification, including the AEAI-VKF hail register. It certifies that a material or product, such as a roof tile, facade component or solar panel, can withstand impacts from hailstones at least 50 mm in diameter, traveling at around 100 to 110 km/h, without visible damage or loss of function.
The requirement would represent a significant increase over the standard IEC 61215 module certification, which tests resistance to hailstones measuring 25 mm in diameter. For hailstones of the same shape, doubling the diameter increases their mass eightfold.
Against a backdrop of more frequent hail events and growing reluctance among insurers to cover exposed installations, the proposed requirement could exclude many modules currently eligible for the reduced VAT rate. The French manufacturer Voltec Solar’s Tarka L11OR 500 W module, in its Diamant version, is cited as a notable exception.
For installers and distributors, the timing is significant because the new rules could take effect the day after publication. Subject to any transitional provisions for sales already agreed, modules without RG5 certification would no longer qualify for the reduced rate.
For quotations already accepted at the 5.5% rate, FNES recommends that installers collect initial deposits without delay and check that modules have valid certification. Installers should also ask suppliers which module models hold RG5 certification to prepare for future sales.
The decree of Sept. 8, 2025, which extended the 5.5% VAT rate to residential solar installations of up to 9 kW from Oct. 1, 2025, already imposed several conditions. These included a module carbon footprint below 530 kg of CO2 equivalent per kW, limits on silver, lead and cadmium content, and an energy management system.
The forthcoming decree would add installation by a qualified or certified company and introduce tighter checks on carbon-footprint calculations and measures to combat fraud.

title: Algeria’s solar capacity surpasses 1 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Analysis by Rystad Energy finds that Algeria has added 760 MW of solar capacity this year following the commissioning of three major projects. International financing, grid expansion and regular procurement rounds will be key to achieving its 15 GW renewables target by 2035.
Patrick Jowett
24 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Utility-scale
Algeria’s installed solar capacity has exceeded 1 GW, according to analysis by
Rystad Energy
The country has inaugurated three large-scale solar projects this year, the latest of which, the
300 MW El Oued Foulia solar plant
, is now its largest operational PV facility. These three plants have added 760 MW of solar already this year, Rystad Energy says, more than Algeria had installed in total by the end of last year.
Surpassing the 1 GW milestone marks a step toward Algeria’s target of deploying
15 GW of renewables
Algeria’s next interim target is to add a further 2 GW of solar capacity in 2027. Nivedh Thaikoottathil, Senior Analyst, Renewables & Power at Rystad Energy, told
pv magazine
the target is achievable as it is supported by an existing project pipeline rather than new projects that still need to be tendered.
“Government-led procurement with [state-owned utility] Sonelgaz’s 1 GW scheme and a
2 GW tender
translated policy ambitions into executable projects,” he explained. “With Sonelgaz being the owner it avoids power purchase agreement (PPA) bankability questions, giving greater speed and certainty.”
Thaikoottathil said meeting next year’s 2 GW target will depend on the timely completion of substations and transmission infrastructure, particularly in southern Algeria, as well as effective coordination between Sonelgaz and engineering, procurement and construction contractors. Equipment supply, customs procedures and local-content requirements could also cause delays, while mobilization and site management in remote areas present additional challenges.
“State-backed procurement reduces commercial uncertainty, while continued funding and project supervision should support delivery,” Thaikoottathil said. “Strong political backing also helps prioritize resources, but it can produce overly optimistic announced completion dates.”
Shifting toward tenders
Thaikoottathil suggested that in order to reach the 15 GW by 2035 target, Algeria needs to shift from its state-funded first phase to an externally-financed, regularly-tendered second phase.
“Operational solar PV, along with the 2 GW targeted for 2027, and a 0.2 GW wind tender cover only about 23% of the 15 GW target,” he told
pv magazine
. “Closing the gap means adding more than 1.4 GW a year from 2028 to 2035.”
Regular, rolling auctions of 1.5 GW to 2 GW will be important to sustaining deployment, alongside standardized PPAs, faster permitting and payment security from Sonelgaz, he added.
Grid infrastructure will also need to keep pace with capacity additions. A planned 800 km north-south transmission line and energy storage will be necessary to reduce the risk of curtailment, Thaikoottathil said, with external financing needed to support these investments.
He also suggested Algeria looks to develop its local assembly capabilities. The country currently has close to 860 MW of solar module assembly capacity, below the more than 1.4 GW of annual capacity additions needed to meet the proposed deployment pace.
“Reliance on international equipment suppliers and contractors creates exposure to import delays, logistics and currency risks,” he said.
Financing the next phase
With international independent power producers and private investors expected to play an increasingly important role in Algeria’s solar expansion, Thaikoottathil said access to international financing could “probably be the single biggest determinant of the 2028-2035 ramp-up”.
He identified Algeria’s dependence on hydrocarbon revenues as one of the risks facing future project development. Lower oil and gas revenues could constrain government funding for new solar projects and the associated grid infrastructure.
Meanwhile, currency and payment risks could also complicate efforts to attract international lenders and investors.
“If revenues are in dinars and debt is in dollars or euros, lenders will want hard-currency indexation, a currency clause or a convertibility guarantee,” Thaikoottathil explained to
pv magazine
. “Algeria maintains foreign-exchange controls, and international investors may face administrative delays in converting revenues and repatriating profits.”
He added that international lenders need confidence that electricity payments will be made reliably over the project lifetime.
“Without adequate payment guarantees, currency protection and predictable contracts, financing costs could remain elevated,” Thaikoottathil said. “Limited access to international capital could hinder progress toward the [15 GW] target.”
C&I, residential growth
While Algeria’s solar expansion is currently being driven by large-scale utility projects, its smaller PV market segments are also expected to develop gradually, Thaikoottathil told
pv magazine
Growth in the C&I market segment is likely to be driven by industrial self-consumption and decarbonization, while off-grid installations could benefit from rural electrification and agricultural demand. Public-sector rooftop solar is another potential growth area, Thaikoottathil said, supported by government programs.
Developments in the residential solar market are expected to remain slower due to subsidized electricity tariffs, high upfront costs and limited financial incentives.
To accelerate deployment across these segments, Thaikoottathil suggested Algeria could introduce investment subsidies, tax benefits and low-interest loans to improve project economics, particularly for C&I customers and households.
“Simpler permitting and grid-connection procedures through Sonelgaz’s distribution companies, with fixed processing timelines, could further develop these small-scale segments,” he recommended.
Other measures could include gradual electricity tariff reform, starting with high-consumption users while protecting vulnerable households, Thaikoottathil said, as well as import-duty or VAT relief and concessional green loans for solar-plus-storage systems.

title: Gokin Solar launches 510 W all-black BC panel with 25.0% efficiency - pv magazine Global

Technology & Products
The Chinese manufacturer’s new double-glass, all-black modules are designed for high-end rooftop applications across Europe. They feature a temperature coefficient of -0.26% per C and a 30-year linear power output guarantee.
Emiliano Bellini
24 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Residential
The GK-3-54HGFDb module
Chinese solar module manufacturer Gokin Solar has presented a new series of full-black solar panels based on back-contact cell technology at the Genera trade show in Madrid, Spain.
The company’s sales manager for the European region, Gloria Luo, told
pv magazine
that the new panels were designed primarily for high-end rooftop applications, where both aesthetics and module dimensions are important considerations. “The panels will be available across all European markets,” she said.
The panels rely on the company’s proprietary GBC technology, which utilizes lightly doped, high-resistivity n-type silicon wafers. According to the manufacturer, the cell architecture places all electrodes on the rear side, eliminating front-side metallization shading and increasing the active light-receiving area by around 1.1%.
The GK-3-54HGFDb series comprises five versions with power outputs ranging from 480 W to 510 W and power conversion efficiencies ranging from 23.5% to 25.0%.
All versions of the panel measure 1,800 mm x 1,134 mm x 30 mm and weigh 24.8 kg. They feature 108 cells arranged in a 6 x 18 configuration, two layers of 2 mm coated semi-tempered glass, a black anodized aluminum frame, and an IP68-rated junction box.
Luo said the company is also offering a version of the product with a black frame rather than a full-black design, depending on customer requirements and price considerations.
The open-circuit voltage ranges from 40.44 V to 40.84 V and the short-circuit current is between 14.78 A and 15.18 A.
The panels have a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V and a temperature coefficient of -0.26% per C. The temperature coefficients for the open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current are -0.22% per C and 0.05% per C, respectively.
The modules can withstand front and rear static loads of up to 5,400 Pa and 2,400 Pa, respectively. They have also undergone hailstone testing with 25 mm diameter hailstones at a speed of 23 m/s, according to the datasheet.
The new products come with a 25-year product warranty and a 30-year linear power output guarantee. The modules are guaranteed to retain 99% of their nominal power output after the first year and 88.85% after 30 years, corresponding to an annual degradation rate of 0.35% after the first year.
Gokin Solar operates four production bases in China, including a module manufacturing facility in Guangzhou, in Guangdong province. According to its website, it currently has an annual production capacity of 100 GW each for silicon ingots and wafers and 16 GW for solar modules.

title: Felicity Solar showcases 20 kWh low-voltage residential battery - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Chinese manufacturer’s new lithium iron phosphate battery features a maximum charging power of 10.2 kW, a maximum discharging power of 12.8 kW, and a depth of discharge of 95%. Up to 15 units can be connected in parallel for a total storage capacity of 300 kWh.
Emiliano Bellini
24 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Residential
The FLA48392TG2-EU battery
China-based battery manufacturer Felicity Solar unveiled a new low-voltage battery energy storage system for residential and small-scale commercial and industrial (C&I) applications at the Genera trade show in Madrid, Spain.
“This product is for the whole world,” Qiqi Zheng, regional director at Felicity Solar, told
pv magazin
, noting that that the adoption of higher-capacity cells is intended to address increasing household electricity consumption.
Dubbed FLA48392TG2-EU, the new product belongs to the company’s FLA series and utilizes lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) cells with a capacity of 392 Ah, providing a nominal energy storage capacity of 20 kWh.
The battery has a nominal voltage of 51.2 V and an operating voltage range of 44.8 V to 57.6 V. Its recommended charging and discharging currents are 100 A and 125 A, respectively, while its maximum charging and discharging currents are 200 A and 250 A, respectively. The system supports a peak current of 300 A for two minutes and has a maximum charging power of 10.2 kW and a maximum discharging power of 12.8 kW.
The floor-mounted battery measures 960 mm x 450 mm x 265 mm and weighs 150.5 kg. It features an IP21-rated enclosure and a depth of discharge of 95%. Its operating temperature ranges from 0 C to 55 C during charging and from -20 C to 55 C during discharging.
The system integrates a battery management system (BMS), a fuse, a circuit breaker, and an aerosol-based fire suppression system. Zheng said the battery, like the company’s other storage products, incorporates multiple levels of protection and features LED and LCD displays that allow users to monitor the battery’s state of charge (SOC).
The device also supports CAN 2.0, RS485, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth communication. “It can be 15 units in parallel,” Zheng said, referring to the system’s scalability to 300 kWh, which also makes it suitable for small-scale C&I installations.
The regional director noted that the company has already deployed multiple units of its existing 16 kWh low-voltage battery in parallel in Spain, demonstrating the potential of its residential storage technology for larger-scale applications.
Felicity Solar claims the new battery has a lifespan of at least 10,000 cycles at 25 C. The company offers a 10-year warranty and lists a cumulative energy throughput of 62 MWh, based on a residual capacity of 60% at the end of life.
Founded in 2007 and headquartered in Guangzhou, southern China, Felicity Solar manufactures solar inverters, lithium batteries, and energy storage systems for residential and C&I applications. The company established its first overseas subsidiary in Nigeria in 2016 and expanded into the European market in 2022, with operations in Germany and the Netherlands.

title: Differ Power unveils '9-in-1' solar-storage heat pump - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Chinese company has developed a residential heat pump system integrating a 6 kW hybrid inverter and supporting battery storage. The propane-based system comes in three versions with heating capacities ranging from 12 kW to 16 kW and can deliver hot water at temperatures of up to 75 C.
Emiliano Bellini
24 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Heat pumps
Residential
The D Series heat pump
Differ Power has unveiled a “9-in-1” air-to-water heat pump system for residential applications at Spain’s Genera trade show. The system combines space heating, cooling and domestic hot water production with PV power inversion, battery management, a power conversion system (PCS), backup power supply, a home energy management system (HEMS) and communication gateway functionality.
Dubbed D Series, the new product was specifically designed for the European residential market and integrates a single-phase hybrid inverter directly into the heat pump unit.
“The most obvious feature is that we put the hybrid inverter inside the heat pump,” Differ Power’s European Product and Technical Director, Schaochen Ji, told
pv magazine
. “The biggest problem for inverters is ventilation.”
Ji explained that the integration enables the inverter to benefit from the heat pump’s ventilation system, reducing thermal stress on its electronic components and potentially extending its operational lifetime.
“For a 6 kW inverter, heat is no longer a problem. The lifespan of the inverter will be significantly extended,” he added.
According to Ji, the system was conceived to address the growing convergence of residential PV and heat pump installations in Europe, particularly in the context of building energy efficiency upgrades.
“When you do an energy efficiency upgrade, most of the time you consider the PV installation and the heat pump at the same time. So why not put them together?” he said.
The new heat pump uses propane (R290) as the refrigerant and features a twin-rotary DC inverter compressor, an electronic expansion valve and a brushless DC fan motor.
It comes in three versions with nominal heating capacities of 12.14 kW, 14.02 kW and 16.04 kW at an outdoor temperature of 7 C and an outlet water temperature of 35 C. The coefficient of performance (COP) ranges from 4.57 to 4.82. At an outlet water temperature of 55 C, the heating capacity ranges from 12.16 kW to 15.84 kW, with a COP of between 3.0 and 3.09.
The systems have a seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) ranging from 5.06 to 5.11 at an outlet water temperature of 35 C and from 3.96 to 3.99 at 55 C. All three models have an A+++ energy efficiency rating at both temperature levels, according to the manufacturer.
The integrated hybrid inverter supports a maximum PV array capacity of 12 kW and a maximum PV input power of 9 kW. It features two maximum power point trackers (MPPTs), each supporting a maximum input current of 16 A, with an MPPT voltage range of 90 V to 550 V.
The inverter has a rated AC output power of 6 kW, a maximum efficiency of 97.5% and a European efficiency of 97%. It also provides a backup output of 6 kVA, with a peak apparent power of 9 kVA for 10 seconds.
The system can be coupled with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries with nominal storage capacities ranging from 7.68 kWh to 15.36 kWh. The batteries have an operating voltage range of 80 V to 460 V, an IP55 protection rating and a claimed cycle life of at least 8,000 cycles. Up to 12 battery clusters can be connected in parallel.
According to Differ Power, the direct use of solar and battery power can increase overall system efficiency by more than 10%, while its smart energy management technology can enable PV self-consumption rates of up to 96%.
All three heat pump models measure 1,300 mm x 990 mm x 575 mm and have sound power levels ranging from 59 dB(A) to 60 dB(A). Each unit contains 1 kg of R290 refrigerant.
The devices can operate at ambient temperatures ranging from -25 C to 45 C in heating mode and from 5 C to 45 C in cooling mode. They can deliver water at temperatures ranging from 20 C to 75 C in heating mode and from 5 C to 25 C in cooling mode.
The system features Wi-Fi connectivity and can be monitored and controlled via an LCD interface, a mobile app, a web portal or a wired controller. According to the product datasheet, certification under the G99, CEI 0-21 and EN 50549 grid standards is in progress.
Ji said the company plans to sell the product through distributors and large installers, without bundling it with solar modules.
“For now, because it has a single-phase inverter inside, we are focusing on Spain, France, Italy and the UK,” he said, adding that the company plans to introduce a three-phase version targeting the German market in 2027.
Differ Power is based in Shenzhen, in China’s Guangdong province, and specializes in integrated residential energy systems combining PV, battery storage, heat pumps and electric vehicle (EV) charging technologies. The company operates a research and development center in Shenzhen and a manufacturing and logistics hub in Foshan.

title: Pilot line recovers high-purity silver, silicon from PV panels - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers have tested two routes for separating the layers of end-of-life solar panels on a pilot recycling line, recovering silver and silicon at purities above 99.99% and finding that a shockwave-based process also preserves a layer the heat-based route destroys.
Brian Publicover
24 Nov 2026
Research & Development
recycling
A research team led by academics from Poland’s AGH University of Krakow has found that separating solar panel layers with shockwaves, rather than heat, preserves more material while still yielding high-purity silver and silicon.
Prof. Pradeep Padhamnath of AGH University of Krakow and three collaborators said they recovered silver at above 99.99% purity and silicon at above 99.995% from end-of-life PV panels on pilot recycling lines, using either heat or shockwaves to separate the layers.
The researchers compared a thermal process with electrohydraulic fragmentation (EHF), a shockwave-based separation process. Only EHF recovered the laminating layer around the solar cells completely; the thermal process lost it.
The backsheet, the protective polymer layer on the rear of a module, was recovered at room temperature before the layers were separated.
The scientists also looked at whether EHF could be integrated into an existing PV recycling pilot line, assessing its compatibility and setting out its advantages and challenges.
“Further developments in recycling of polymers and material processing could result in entirely closed-loop recycling of EOL PV panels,” said the research team.
Earlier work
The pilot-line study builds on the group’s
2025 paper in
Solar Energy
. In that study, the researchers described EHF as a process in which electrodes connected to a power supply of about 50 kV create an arc in water, generating shockwaves that separate the panel’s layers. They tested laboratory-made glass-glass, glass-backsheet and glass-free panels for 240, 480 or 720 seconds.
The group’s earlier work describes the thermal route as heating panels to about 450 C to 550 C to decompose polymers such as EVA, PVDF and PET, separating the glass, metallic ribbons and solar cells.
In the 2025 study, the scientists cited EHF’s room-temperature operation, its lack of toxic emissions and its ability to recover polymers that would otherwise be burned in pyrolysis. They also found the process was sensitive to feed size and could clog when overloaded. EVA did not fully separate from the backsheet, glass-free panels separated poorly, and some fine powder was lost.
The scientists described their latest findings in “
Design of pilot lines with thermal and electrohydraulic fragmentation delamination routes and analysis of materials recovered from end-of-life silicon PV panels
,” which was recently published in
Waste Management
Silver is the main driver of recycling economics. It accounts for just 0.03% of a panel’s mass but can be worth more than the
glass, aluminum and silicon
combined, according to Fraunhofer CSP. Other pilot-scale delamination work includes a
high-pressure water-jet method
that recovered silver at 97% purity. An IEA-PVPS report published in May found that recovery rates for high-value materials have
improved significantly
since a 2024 study, in which the benchmark mechanical recycling technology recovered no silicon or silver.

content:
Markets & Policy
With Cyprus having more than 1 GW of installed solar capacity against average electricity demand of around 650 MW, its government is looking to accelerate storage deployment to address rising solar curtailment and improve grid flexibility.
Patrick Jowett
24 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Cyprus is planning to deploy more than 300 MW of battery storage capacity across its electricity system as it seeks to reduce ongoing curtailment of solar power.
Speaking at the 14th Cyprus Energy Symposium, the country’s Energy, Commerce and Industry Minister Michael Damianos identified energy storage, electricity interconnection and market reforms as the three main pillars of the government’s strategy to address growing pressure on its electricity system.
Damianos told attendees of the symposium that Cyprus has more than 1,040 MW of installed solar capacity, compared with average electricity demand of approximately 650 MW.
This imbalance means the country is forced to curtail renewable electricity during periods of high solar generation while continuing to rely heavily on imported oil.
Solar curtailment in Cyprus hit
47% in 2025
and increased further over the first five months of 2026,
reaching 65%
. The country’s storage market is still in its relative infancy with its
first utility battery project
, a 5 MWh facility tied to a 1.8 MW solar array, entering the market in August.
During his speech, Damianos confirmed the first 120 MW of grid-connected storage being developed by the transmission system operator is expected to be operational by summer 2027.
He added that the state-owned utility Electricity Authority of Cyprus is developing
80 MW of storage capacity
at its Dhekelia power station, targeted for 2027, and revealed a further 100 MW is planned at Moni power station.
“These investments will reduce renewable energy curtailments, increase system flexibility and allow greater integration of renewables,” Damianos said.
The minister’s speech comes as several battery projects installed earlier this year are still
waiting for grid connections
in order to begin operations.
Damianos also discussed electricity market reforms designed to encourage more flexible consumption and investment. Cyprus’ competitive electricity market became operational in October 2025, while new rooftop solar installations
transitioned from net metering
to a market-based self-consumption framework in January this year.
He said Cyprus must also look to electrify heating, cooling and transport through heat pumps, electric vehicles and smart charging to turn midday solar surpluses into economic value. “This requires electricity tariffs that reward flexibility, faster grid connections and substantial investment in electricity networks,” he said.
Damianos also addressed electricity interconnection. As the only EU member state that remains electrically isolated, Cyprus considers the
Great Sea Interconnector
, which is planned to link Greece, Cyprus and Israel, a strategic priority.
The project could “strengthen security of supply, enable two-way electricity flows, improve grid stability and facilitate greater renewable energy integration,” the minister said.
“It will also open up electricity export opportunities, reduce emissions and make our electricity system more competitive. Cyprus remains committed to advancing the project in cooperation with Greece and the European Union, while ensuring its technical and economic viability,” he added.

title: Bangladesh developer plans 45 MW solar plant with foreign funding - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
A Bangladeshi power producer and an international infrastructure investor plan to build a 45 MW solar plant in Chittagong district at a cost of about $45 million, with output sold to the state utility.
Syful Islam
24 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
Bangladeshi conglomerate Baraka Group and international infrastructure investment firm Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG) have agreed to jointly set up a 45 MW solar power plant in Fatikchhari subdistrict, in Bangladesh’s Chittagong district.
The plant will be built at a cost of around $45 million, mainly with foreign investment. The project is expected to come online within two years, the company said in Dhaka on Nov. 19. It has signed a 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with the Bangladesh Power Development Board.
Baraka Power already supplies 265 MW of electricity to the national grid. The group also has businesses in the apparel, healthcare, securities, and education sectors.
Faisal Ahmed Chowdhury, chairman of Baraka Power, said the project is being implemented through large-scale investment in foreign currency, which will have a positive impact on the country’s economy.
“PIDG’s investments in Bangladesh’s power and renewable energy sectors would continue to grow in the future,” he said.
He also said the company is committed to implementing more eco-friendly power projects, in line with the government’s goal of generating 20% of electricity from renewable sources by 2030.
PIDG has previously invested in Bangladesh’s renewable energy and agriculture sectors. In 2020, it arranged loans for the country’s first utility-scale solar plant, the 20 MW Teknaf Solartech facility.
“The project had significant market-level benefits: it now serves as an open-source framework to inspire replication by other developers, and also serves as a case study for local lenders,” said PIDG.
Bangladesh now has 2,210 MW of renewable generation capacity, including 1,917 MW of solar.
To boost clean power generation, the government has introduced several policy measures in recent months. These include cutting the tax on solar equipment imports from 17% to 1% for 180 days and introducing a BDT 10.50 ($0.084)/kWh tariff for surplus electricity from eligible rooftop solar systems under its net-metering regime.

title: Solar and storage insolvencies hit larger German companies - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Solar and storage companies accounted for 10 of Germany’s 103 major corporate insolvencies in the third quarter of 2026, with cases increasingly involving project developers and battery manufacturers alongside installers and distributors, according to consultancy Falkensteg.
Sandra Enkhardt
24 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Bankruptcies
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Ten major insolvencies in Germany’s photovoltaic and energy storage sectors were recorded in the third quarter of 2026, according to an analysis by transformation consultancy Falkensteg. The company defines a major insolvency as a filing by a business with annual revenue exceeding €10 million ($10.9 million).
A total of 103 companies filed for insolvency between July and September, down 3% from the previous quarter and 18% year on year, according to Falkensteg’s quarterly report, published on Monday.
Photovoltaic and storage companies accounted for almost 10% of those cases, a significant increase from two in the second quarter of 2026 and seven in the same period a year earlier. Although the sector recorded 13 major insolvencies in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 16 in the same period of 2025, the size and distribution of the affected businesses have changed.
Alongside installation and trading companies, project developers and battery storage manufacturers are now facing insolvency proceedings. Falkensteg’s analysis found that four of the 10 cases involved solar and wind project developers, three involved battery and storage system manufacturers, and three involved installation and trading companies.
Two of the 10 companies, Enerparc and Varta, each had group revenue exceeding €750 million, making them the largest insolvency cases of the quarter by revenue, Falkensteg said. However, Varta’s residential photovoltaic storage business is not included in its insolvency proceedings.
The reasons for the filings also differed. Varta cited a financing shortfall at its parent company, weaker demand and the loss of a key customer. Enerparc, meanwhile, was unable to secure financing for battery storage projects.
Falkensteg partner Jonas Eckhardt, who authored the report, said the number of cases had fallen but the largest insolvencies had become more significant. While installation companies were particularly affected in 2025, project developers and battery storage manufacturers have increasingly come under pressure in 2026.
Eckhardt said the storage market was expanding rapidly while newly installed photovoltaic capacity had stagnated. Both business models require substantial capital, while revenues can fluctuate considerably. He identified financing as the main constraint, adding that uncertainty over Germany’s planned amendments to its Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG) and its grid package was making projects difficult to assess and finance.
Falkensteg expects further major insolvencies in the current quarter. Sonnen and Energiekonzepte Deutschland, among others, filed for preliminary insolvency proceedings in October. However, Eckhardt does not expect the sector to reach its 2025 total of 21 insolvency filings by the end of this year.

title: Residential solar linked to reduced health risks from extreme temperatures - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Research from Japan finds residential solar installations can offer protection against heat-related mortality by making electricity more affordable for households to run air conditioning.
Patrick Jowett
24 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Highlights
Residential
Rooftops in Japan
Residential solar installations can mitigate the mortality risks associated with extremely hot temperatures, according to new research.
Researchers Yi-Chun Ko from the Asian Growth Research Institute and Shinsuke Uchida from Japan’s Doshisha University explored how residential solar can make electricity more affordable to run air conditioning when electricity prices spike due to factors such as supply disruptions, geopolitical shocks or extremely hot weather.
Their findings are presented in the research paper
Climate resilience through residential solar energy: Reducing health risks from extreme temperatures
, available in the journal
Social Science & Medicine.
According to Uchida, it marks the “first causal evidence that household solar PV can also work as a public health intervention, reducing heat-related mortality through improved energy affordability”.
Ko and Uchida used the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake as a natural experiment. The shutdown of nuclear power plants following the earthquake contributed to electricity price increases of up to 38%, while Japan simultaneously promoted residential solar PV through a nationwide subsidy program.
The pair combined monthly prefecture-level mortality data from 44 Japanese prefectures between 2009 and 2014 with weather data and official solar installation figures. They then used an instrumental variable approach to isolate the effects of solar PV adoption from other factors that might influence household health outcomes.
The results showed that residential solar PV adoption significantly reduced mortality associated with extreme heat, with the greatest impact observed among people aged 65 and above.
Based on the annual average growth rate of solar PV installations during the study period, the researchers estimated that excess deaths associated with extremely hot days were reduced by approximately 8.2% annually for the overall population and 8.5% for people aged 65 and above.
The protective effects of residential solar were also stronger in warmer prefectures, those that experienced greater electricity price increases following the 2011 earthquake, and areas subject to stricter energy conservation targets. No comparable effects were observed at cold temperatures, which the researchers attributed to solar PV’s stronger generation profile during sunnier and warmer weather.
Analysis from the research paper says these findings “show that distributed renewable energy provides direct health protection during climate extremes”.
“By relaxing households’ electricity affordability constraints, solar PV improves their ability to maintain safe indoor environments when cooling demand is highest,” it explains. “Our findings reframe residential solar PV from a primarily environmental intervention into a multifaceted tool for climate resilience that addresses the interlinked challenges of energy security, public health, and climate adaptation.”
The paper adds that as climate change increases heat exposure worldwide, adaptation strategies will depend on reliable and affordable access to energy progressively more.
“Distributed renewable energy offers one pathway through which households can buffer climate risk by reducing their dependence on grid supply when cooling is most critical and centralised systems face price volatility or supply constraints,” the researchers wrote.
The paper also points out that as residential solar adoption remains skewed towards areas with more higher-income households, any associated health benefits may accrue unevenly. It also warns that in ageing societies where older people on fixed incomes face heightened vulnerability to heat exposures, unequal access to self-generation technologies, such as residential solar, could end up amplifying climate-related health disparities.
The researchers therefore called for targeted policies to ensure the health benefits reach vulnerable populations most at risk from rising temperatures and energy costs.
Uchida said the findings “show that homes that generate their own electricity can become part of the infrastructure that protects public health”.

title: Claude claims to prove VP ≠ VNP in Valiant's 47-year-old conjecture
content: Anthropic has published a 70-page mathematical paper credited entirely to Claude, claiming to settle a longstanding problem in algebraic complexity theory. The research targets Valiant’s conjecture, a mathematical counterpart to the famous P versus NP problem.An internal research model reportedly discovered the result before producing a formal proof using Lean 4. Anthropic has published both documents in its GitHub repository, making the work available for independent examination. However, no human mathematician has reviewed the proof so far.The paper, titled “VP ≠ VNP over every field,” claims to establish that VP is strictly contained within VNP across every field. If correct, the result would resolve a major open question in algebraic complexity theory. It would not, however, settle the broader P versus NP problem.Difficult computational problemAt the center of the research lies the permanent, a mathematical expression closely related to the determinant of a matrix. Both involve multiplying selected matrix entries and adding the resulting products. However, their mathematical properties produce very different computational challenges.The determinant allows efficient calculations through established mathematical techniques. The permanent lacks an equivalent shortcut, making its computation considerably more difficult as matrix dimensions increase.For example, a 13-by-13 matrix produces billions of terms in its permanent expansion. Calculating every term individually becomes impractical as matrices grow larger.An internal Claude model just found a proof of the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, known as Valiant’s conjectureClaude is credited as the author of the 70-page paper and the Lean proof passed automated checks.If you remember the determinant of a 2×2 matrix, it’s ad − bc.… pic.twitter.com/v9Sa6euxVE— alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv) November 23, 2026The research claims that arithmetic circuits cannot overcome this difficulty through efficient combinations of additions and multiplications. Its results establish superpolynomial lower bounds on the number of operations required.Specifically, circuits computing the permanent of an m-by-m matrix require more than m raised to c times the logarithm of m raised to one-third. Here, c represents a positive constant, and the bound applies to sufficiently large matrices.The same lower bound applies to the permanent over fields with characteristics other than two. The Hamiltonian cycle polynomial also satisfies this bound across every field.Why the distinction mattersValiant introduced the VP versus VNP problem in 1979. These complexity classes describe the computational difficulty of evaluating families of mathematical polynomials.VP broadly represents problems that arithmetic circuits can solve efficiently. VNP encompasses a wider class of problems whose solutions admit efficient verification through algebraic computations.The relationship resembles the distinction between P and NP in conventional computational complexity. However, the two frameworks examine different computational models.Arithmetic circuits operate on mathematical values across an entire field, including its extensions. Boolean circuits, meanwhile, process binary inputs and use logical operations.That difference explains why the claimed result does not resolve P versus NP. A lower bound for arithmetic circuits does not automatically establish equivalent limitations for Boolean circuits.The permanent provides a particularly important example. Its computational difficulty contrasts with the determinant, which has efficient polynomial-size arithmetic circuits.Lean verification has limitsAnthropic has also published a Lean 4 formalization alongside the research paper. Lean is a proof assistant that checks mathematical arguments against formally specified statements.The formalization allows automated systems to examine whether individual proof steps follow from the preceding mathematical statements. Its inclusion provides another way to scrutinize the extensive argument.However, successful automated checks do not establish that the formalized statements accurately represent every claim in the paper. That distinction remains important when evaluating the research.Anthropic explicitly acknowledges that no human mathematician has checked the proof. The repository also warns that no machine verifies whether the formalized statement fully matches the intended conclusion.Independent mathematical scrutiny will therefore play an essential role in establishing the result’s credibility. Until researchers examine the argument and its formalization, the claimed resolution remains unconfirmed.Even with those limitations, the publication presents an unusual research milestone. An internal Claude model reportedly developed the argument, wrote the paper, and produced its formal verification files.The mathematical community now has an opportunity to examine a machine-generated attempt at resolving a problem that has remained open for decades.

title: US fires 24 rounds in third successful test of reusable rocket system
content: Lockheed Martin has put a new rocket training system through its third successful flight test, moving closer to a potential replacement for the U.S. Army’s existing practice rockets. The demonstration involved firing 24 training rounds from a High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) launcher.The November test took place at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona. It evaluated the Joint Reduced Range Rocket (JR3), a training system designed to make live-fire exercises more affordable. Its reusable launch hardware could help the Army conduct more frequent rocket drills without relying on expensive operational ammunition.The JR3 program targets U.S. Army requirements and could eventually serve international military partners. Lockheed Martin is developing the system around established rocket motor technology. Its design focuses on reducing the cost of repeated training exercises while retaining realistic firing characteristics.New approach to trainingRocket artillery crews need regular live-fire exercises to maintain proficiency. However, training with operational ammunition can place considerable pressure on military budgets. Range availability and ammunition costs also limit how frequently crews can practice.JR3 aims to address those challenges through a purpose-built training round. Its rocket motor uses established technology, helping avoid the expense of developing an entirely new propulsion system.The system also features an adaptable payload that produces visible marking effects. These effects allow instructors to evaluate rocket placement during exercises. The November demonstration examined the rocket’s range, flight path, and accuracy.Lockheed Martin previously conducted another successful JR3 flight test in August. That demonstration involved launching rockets from a HIMARS launcher. The November exercise expanded the testing with a complete 24-round salvo.Reusable launch hardware mattersOne of JR3’s most interesting engineering features involves its launch infrastructure. The system pairs individual training rounds with a reusable 24-round rocket launch pod.Its reloadable launch tubes allow crews to reuse critical launch hardware across multiple training cycles. That approach could lower the overall expense of maintaining regular live-fire programs.JR3 also supports both HIMARS and M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System launchers. These platforms give the Army flexibility when organizing artillery training across different units.The system’s design also addresses environmental flexibility. Lockheed Martin intends JR3 to support exercises across different locations and operating conditions. Crews could conduct realistic firing drills during daylight or nighttime training sessions.Sabrina Barnes, vice president of Lockheed Martin Precision Fires Rockets, described affordability as a central design priority.“Our new training round offers a scalable, very affordable solution built on mature rocket motor technology,” Barnes said.She added that the 24-round launch pod addresses the Army’s demand for greater training volume. The system aims to deliver that capacity without compromising performance.Future applications beyond trainingJR3 remains under development, but its modular design could offer applications beyond conventional training exercises. Lockheed Martin says the architecture could support future efforts involving inexpensive, mass-producible rockets.That possibility makes the program relevant beyond its immediate replacement objective. A modular approach could allow developers to adapt existing components for different requirements. However, Lockheed Martin has not announced specific operational applications for such future variants.The Army’s eventual adoption will depend on further development and testing. The three successful demonstrations provide evidence of the system’s flight performance. Further evaluation will determine how effectively JR3 meets military training requirements.Its central proposition remains straightforward: give artillery crews more opportunities to practice without consuming expensive operational rockets. The reusable launch pod and established motor technology form the foundation of that approach.

title: OpenAI's Codex builds shields to block exploits on Linux systems
content: OpenAI and Cisco have launched an open-source security runtime that can protect running Linux systems from cyberattacks while teams prepare permanent software patches.Called Shirudo, the project uses a Linux technology known as extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) to deploy temporary security protections, called shields, against vulnerable code paths without restarting affected services.In a controlled demonstration, a shield generated using OpenAI’s Codex blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service. The protection rejected malicious input while allowing the application to continue operating without a restart, OpenAI said.The project targets a persistent challenge in cybersecurity. Testing and deploying software patches can take days or weeks, leaving systems exposed to attacks during the waiting period. Blocking the underlying Linux operation entirely can also disrupt legitimate requests and potentially take applications offline.Shirudo is designed to address this gap by allowing security teams to test targeted safeguards against malicious activity while checking whether legitimate workloads continue functioning. Operators retain control over deployment and must approve a shield before it becomes active.How Shirudo protects LinuxShirudo uses eBPF, which allows small programs to run at specific points inside the Linux operating system kernel without modifying its source code. The technology can observe system and network activity and apply targeted protections to running applications.OpenAI and Cisco are developing the runtime to help security agents investigate vulnerabilities, generate shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads.The system incorporates several safeguards before protections are deployed. Each shield is cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux’s eBPF verifier also checks programs against its safety requirements, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.Shirudo also uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to maintain a verifiable record of security protections being loaded or removed. This gives operators additional evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.Cisco said testing against Java4Shell and a separate PHP vulnerability demonstrated the system’s ability to generate code that detects and blocks exploitation attempts.“Finding a bug today doesn’t mean you can patch every system tomorrow,” said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI. He said the collaboration would help teams protect systems that need to remain operational while permanent fixes are developed and deployed.Open-source security pushOpenAI and Cisco are releasing Shirudo as an open-source project to encourage developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators to test the runtime and contribute improvements.The software is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, while its eBPF programs are dual-licensed under BSD and GPL terms. Developers can access the code through GitHub and follow the documentation to test and deploy protections in a virtual machine.The companies are also inviting contributors to develop new shields, reproduce vulnerabilities, and test protections against different Linux kernel builds.Beyond temporary safeguards, the collaboration aims to develop infrastructure that can identify vulnerable systems, validate protections, and deploy targeted defenses while maintaining service availability.The longer-term plan includes strengthening operating system security, restricting application permissions and making software updates and recovery safer. The companies also want to improve the ability to contain compromises and restore systems to a verified, known-good state.Shirudo is an early step towards that goal, with its developers inviting the wider security community to help evaluate and improve the runtime.

title: Anthropic mathematician says 250,000-page Riemann proof 'was a joke'
content: Levent Alpöge, the Anthropic mathematician who claimed to have proved the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude, has clarified a detail that attracted widespread attention. The much-discussed figure of 250,000 pages was never meant as a serious description of his mathematical work. Alpöge says he used the enormous number as a joke, amused by how absurdly large it sounded. He has now apologized for allowing the figure to fuel confusion around his announcement.In a follow-up statement, Alpöge explained that he enjoys making jokes about unusually large numbers. He had expected the technical language surrounding his theorem to make the humor apparent. However, readers took the figure literally, and he chose not to address the resulting discussion immediately.The joke behind the numbersAlpöge also referenced an earlier mathematical project involving the Yang-Mills existence problem. He recalled joking about working through 60,000 pages of what he described as unnecessarily complicated material. A committee’s request for a formal Lean version eventually made him question that approach.Stupid things I did:1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on…— levent (@__alpoge__) November 23, 2026His latest clarification also explains why he published computer-checkable Lean code instead of a conventional mathematical paper. He considered a massive, machine-generated explanation unsuitable for publication. Consequently, he chose to release the formalized argument instead.The mathematician acknowledged that the Lean submission contains considerable unnecessary material. Although the code compiles, he accepted that criticism of its organization and quality was justified. He admitted that cleaning it up proved unexpectedly difficult.Proof needs simplifyingAlpöge also addressed criticism from mathematician Scott N. Armstrong about the quality of his mathematical write-up. He acknowledged that producing clear explanations has challenged him throughout his academic career. Some previous theorems took nearly a decade to document properly.He hopes to approach the current work more responsibly. Alpöge suspects that much of the existing argument could eventually disappear through simplification. Waiting for that process might have produced a cleaner submission. However, he chose to publish the existing formalization.His comments also reveal what he considers the central contribution. He argues that the mathematical arguments themselves provide building blocks for developing definitions. Their importance may not immediately register with readers unfamiliar with the underlying mathematics.What the breakthrough meansThe Riemann Hypothesis dates back to 1859 and concerns the distribution of prime numbers. It predicts that every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function lies on a specific vertical line. Mathematicians have investigated the conjecture for more than 160 years.Alpöge previously said Claude helped him develop an argument addressing the hypothesis. His announcement also extended to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. He released the work as a formal Lean submission instead of a conventional research paper.The distinction between a computer-checked argument and a mathematical explanation remains important. Lean can check whether formal reasoning follows from the definitions and assumptions encoded in a submission. However, mathematicians still need to understand the underlying ideas and establish their broader significance.Alpöge says he wants the Riemann Hypothesis to become easier to understand. He believes genuine mathematical difficulty can expose weaknesses in the definitions researchers currently use. His latest comments suggest that simplifying the argument matters more than celebrating its extraordinary length.

title: Tiny atomic flaws could unlock self-healing alloys for fusion reactors
content: Researchers in China have reportedly identified a new way to develop self-healing metal alloys that could withstand radiation damage in nuclear and fusion reactors.The research was carried out by scientists from the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) and Xi’an Jiaotong University in China’s Shaanxi Province. For the study, the team examined multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), which have several metals as their main components.They found that tiny irregularities in the arrangement of atoms can influence how metals respond to radiation damage. This finding could make it easier to develop alloys capable of repairing damage at the atomic level. Guan Pengfei, PhD, a researcher at CAS’ Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology and Engineering (NIMTE), and lead author of the study, stressed that the findings could lead to stronger, longer-lasting materials for nuclear energy and aerospace. “This work offers a new path for designing radiation-resistant alloys for extreme environments,” Guan added. Metals that healMulti-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are materials made by combining several metals, typically three or more, in nearly equal or moderate proportions, instead of relying on one base metal. They include medium-entropy alloys (MEAs), high-entropy alloys (HEAs), and compositionally complex alloys (CCAs).These alloys usually stand out for their strong mechanical properties, resistance to radiation damage, and flexibility in composition. They moreover show promise for applications where traditional metals may not perform well.However, developing them remains challenging, as scientists must examine how different combinations of elements behave when exposed to radiation. This, as a result, can involve a lot of calculations.Lattice distortion narrows the difference in vacancy and interstitial mobility, and promotes the recombination of irradiation-induced defects.Credit: NIMTEAs per the team, radiation can displace atoms out of their normal positions inside a metal. This can lead to two types of defects, such as vacancies, where the atoms are missing from their usual positions, and interstitials, where the displaced atoms occupy spaces between other atoms.When these defects move through the material and meet, they could recombine, and potentially even repair some of the damage. The team found that a property known as local lattice distortion (LLD) plays an important role in this process. LLD refers to small shifts in atoms from their ideal positions within a crystal structure. Faster alloy discoveryTo further investigate the matter, the researchers created a high-fidelity machine-learning model that predicts interactions among atoms in zirconium (Zr), titanium (Ti), and niobium (Nb) alloys. It reproduced results from density functional theory (DFT) and outperformed conventional interatomic potentials.Simulations showed that greater local lattice distortion speeds up the movement of vacancies while slowing down interstitials. This reduces the difference in how quickly the two defects move, and makes it easier for them to recombine.The researchers also confirmed similar behavior in vanadium-cobalt-nickel and nickel-palladium alloys. This suggested that the effect applies to different metal combinations. At the same time, the scientists developed composition–structure that show how alloy composition affects atomic structure. These could identify materials where defects can more easily recombine and repair radiation damage. “We can now screen candidates without expensive calculations for every composition,” Guan concluded in a press release. The study has been published in the journal PNAS on November 20.

title: Anthropic's new safeguards hunt cyber threats without storing data
content: Anthropic has expanded its enterprise security capabilities with a system that can identify sophisticated AI misuse without retaining customer data. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) monitors activity across multiple requests, helping organizations detect coordinated attacks that conventional security filters might miss.The system addresses a growing challenge for businesses adopting autonomous AI agents. Individual requests can appear harmless even when they form part of a larger malicious operation. EFS aims to identify those patterns without requiring Anthropic or cloud providers to store customer information.More than 100 customers have helped develop the system since September. That group includes a quarter of Fortune 100 companies. Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe have also evaluated EFS during its private beta.Tracking threats across multiple requestsTraditional security filters examine individual prompts and responses for potentially harmful activity. Anthropic’s existing classifiers provide this protection through real-time request screening. However, sophisticated attacks can unfold across multiple sessions and involve several AI agents.A coordinated cyber operation illustrates the problem. Anthropic’s September 2026 threat intelligence report described an attack targeting roughly 50 organizations. An AI agent distributed different tasks among multiple agents running simultaneously.Zero data retention (ZDR) with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) is now in public beta for eligible businesses. It looks for misuse across many requests while remaining compatible with ZDR.We developed it with over 100 customers.Read more: https://t.co/M8riFzHDPY pic.twitter.com/eOonILkHt3— Claude (@claudeai) November 23, 2026The operation also retained stolen credentials between sessions. This allowed attackers to resume their activities without repeating earlier steps. Individual requests could have looked like ordinary tasks when examined separately.EFS adds another layer of monitoring to address these threats. Its automated system examines activity patterns across multiple requests. When it identifies suspicious behavior, it generates a Safety Case for the customer’s security team.These reports contain findings without exposing the underlying prompts or responses. Organizations can retrieve them through cloud storage or an API. Security teams can also connect the reports to their existing security information and event management systems.Customer-controlled data storageEFS separates security monitoring from conventional data retention practices. Customers provide their own storage infrastructure for AI inputs and outputs. Anthropic processes the information for automated monitoring without keeping another copy.The system deletes inputs and outputs promptly after transferring them to customer-controlled storage. Organizations also manage access permissions, audit logs, and encryption keys. Neither Anthropic nor cloud provider personnel can access the underlying inputs and outputs.Anthropic also excludes customer data from model and classifier training. Automated safety monitoring represents the only permitted use of that information under EFS.This architecture could help organizations with strict data governance requirements adopt more capable AI systems. Healthcare providers, financial institutions, and legal businesses often face restrictions on sensitive information. EFS offers another approach to monitoring AI activity without introducing conventional data retention.Cloud deployment options expandBusinesses can access EFS through several existing cloud platforms. Supported options include the Claude Platform, Amazon Bedrock, and Claude on Google Cloud. Customers can use Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage within their own accounts.For deployments through Amazon Bedrock and Google-managed Claude, the cloud provider operates the monitoring system. The complete data flow remains within the provider’s cloud environment.Microsoft Foundry support is also in development. Eligible customers will receive deployment instructions from Anthropic. The company also provides technical documentation and a security whitepaper explaining the architecture.Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, and PwC are among the consulting partners supporting EFS deployments.

title: New 173 Ah LFP battery boasts 245 Wh/L, requires no liquid cooling
content: A French company has unveiled a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery for electric excavators, loaders, telehandlers, and agricultural tractors, with an energy density exceeding 245 watt-hours per liter (Wh/L).Forsee Power’s new ZEN 8 battery uses 173 ampere-hour (Ah) LFP cells and does not require liquid cooling. According to the Ivry-sur-Seine-based company it can make electric machinery simpler and less expensive to build. The new battery can also replace Forsee Power’s existing nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) battery without requiring manufacturers to make changes to their vehicles. Christophe Gurtner, Forsee Power CEO and chairman, emphasized the significance of the battery. “With the new ZEN 8 LFP, we are combining exceptional LFP energy density, competitive pricing and European manufacturing in a solution designed for rapid industrial deployment,” Gurtner explained. Inside the new batteryThe ZEN 8 battery uses 173 Ah LFP cells and runs at a nominal module voltage of 45 volts (V). These prismatic cells are commonly used in energy storage systems (ESS), RVs, marine setups, and electric traction. It has an energy density exceeding 245 Wh/L, which means that it could store a considerable amount of energy in a relatively compact space.The ZEN 8 LFP battery. Credit – Forsee PowerAlthough it uses LFP instead of NMC chemistry, it offers the same energy capacity and voltage range as the previous version. Forsee Power said the new design also comes with improved performance, and targets a longer cycle life. What’s more, the battery also eliminates the need for liquid cooling. This process utilizes circulating fluid to remove heat from the batteries, and keeps them within safe operating temperatures, usually between 77 and 104 degrees Fahrenheit (25 and 40 degrees Celsius). However, liquid cooling systems need extra parts, including pumps and pipes, to prevent batteries from overheating. Since the new ZEN 8 battery does not require liquid cooling, manufacturers could build simpler vehicles and reduce production and maintenance costs. The battery also targets a charging rate of 0.7C, which could reduce downtime between daily operations.Built for heavy machinesMostly intended for smaller electric machines for construction, agriculture, waste management, and urban cleaning, the cell could power a range of vehicles. One of its main applications is compact electric street sweepers, with capacities from 50 to 130 kilowatt-hours (kWh) and a target operating time of eight hours.However, the battery also targets smaller excavators, loaders, telehandlers, as well as agricultural tractors. It’s also compatible with existing vehicles, considering that it has the same external dimensions and mounting points as the previous ZEN 8 NMC model. The ZEN 8 LFP battery is manufactured in France. It has been designed to comply with applicable provisions of the EU Battery Regulation, such as CE marketing and battery passport obligations.According to Gurtner, manufacturing the battery in France could also help vehicle makers meet future European requirements for locally made parts, such as those proposed under the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). “We are giving OEMs a simpler, more competitive way to electrify compact machinery while preparing for Europe’s evolving regulatory requirements,” he concluded in a press release.
