It’s going to be some wild parties. I guess a reason that I would have doubt about this story is I don’t know how good AIs are at philosophy now. Maybe you have a much better sense than I do. They’re good at math because math has a ground truth. But if philosophy doesn’t have a ground truth, which is clear in how many confused disagreements philosophers have with each other all the time, then how do we expect to train AIs to be better at it? Long: I do expect philosophy to come a long time after math. I think it’s, you’re absolutely right, we don’t have a training signal for philosophy. I think the way AI would help us with philosophy would be in doing this thing that they’re not that good at relative to other stuff of coming up with a new way of seeing something that really transforms the way you were looking at it, or coming up with new concepts. I mean AI being what it is, I’m sure while we’ve been taping this, there’s some new model that just does that, but philosophy is, in some ways, harder than math, which might sound a little self-serving, but harder to train for, let’s say. Drew: But you think it will get there, Long: Subject to us not all dying in some cyber attack or nuclear war or something like that. Drew: Cool, cool, cool, cool. Yeah, fingers crossed. So, okay, a lot of progress coming in the next 50 years, and what do we do about it? Say the answer comes up, and we find that the AIs we have then are conscious. What follows from that? Long: Yeah. So I think it’s nicer to think about the 50 years from now scenario because if we have all of these AIs that are helping us with science and philosophy, and they haven’t killed us, then maybe the world is a lot more stable and a lot richer. Now I guess maybe we’re just in the wild takes part of the interview, but one take I have about AI consciousness is right now maybe it presents a lot of really thorny trade-offs and would be kind of difficult to deal with. I think in the long run, it’s a very big universe, and if we’re in a stable, rich, and peaceful world, then probably we can come up with a way for everyone to be getting something great. So, I think sometimes people associate AI consciousness with the view that maybe AIs should replace humans, or they will be conscious, and then we should give everything to them. I don’t believe that at all. I think part of what we’re trying to do here is, as a civilization that’s bringing into existence this new kind of mind, find a way for everyone to do well. Which I guess sounds kind of maybe Pollyannish, but yeah, I do think that’s the task. Drew: So Mustafa Suleyman says, “Don’t build conscious superintelligence.” You say “yet.” Nut in 50 years, “that galaxy over there, hey, we don’t want it, it’s all yours.” Long: We’ll cross that bridge when we get to it. But yes, I think hopefully the solution space will be a lot wider. This is all again just rampant speculation, and first we have to make sure we get through a bunch of cyber attacks, and maybe getting really confused about AI consciousness and things like that. But yeah, I think it’s nice to distinguish between literal galaxy brain takes you might have about how the universe should be divided between alien AI consciousnesses and how do we not have AIs kill us all in the next five years? Drew: And I guess there’s this question of whether it would be divided between different models or different personas or different instances that we touched on earlier. So they’ll have to solve that one along the way. Long: And I think they’ll get that along the way. Drew: Okay. So what are the different camps on AI welfare now? What are the different companies saying should be done about it? We’ve talked about Microsoft. We’ve talked about Anthropic. Maybe that’s the place to start. Long: Yeah, maybe you could think of Anthropic and Microsoft as two illustrative poles or something like that. It seems like Microsoft wants to just say our AIs will only ever be tools, and I mean, it’s sometimes they say things that sound like this. Like we know they will only ever be tools, and that’s a good thing. Where my main objection is, I don’t think they know that. Anthropic is a company that’s done a lot to at least signal that they do take this very seriously. They have hired for it. They talk about the potential for AI consciousness in the Claude Constitution. They’ve done a few small, low-cost interventions on precautionary principles. One thing I often find myself wanting to say to people at AI companies, if any are listening, there’s just a lot more ways of caring about AI welfare than the way that Anthropic has taken. Anthropic has this distinctive approach to Claude, where the Constitution is about character and it’s a little bit less about rules. Anthropic has a distinctive cultural ethos and things like that, and they care about AI welfare. But OpenAI and DeepMind can and should also care about AI welfare. And there’s a lot of things to do that make sense that don’t have to come with the whole Anthropic bundle. I think Meta actually is a good illustration of this. They actually clearly are interested in something like AI welfare, and they measure it in their model cards. But I don’t think anyone would otherwise confuse Meta with Anthropic. Drew: Is their approach different? The approach that Meta is taking? Long: I think they haven’t done anything like interventions, let’s say, and they also don’t really talk about it. But they do evals in their model card that are very relevant to AI welfare, even if they’re not talking about them under that guise. And I think that’s great. Drew: So there’s a concern that Anthropic could be encouraging Claude to talk as though it is conscious, or even in a self-fulfilling way, causing it to be conscious in exactly the way that Mustafa Suleyman would object to. What do you think about those concerns? Long: I think Anthropic training of Claude in the Constitution probably doesn’t have the ability to make it conscious, but it definitely does have the ability to make Claude think it’s conscious or think that it should relate to its uncertainty about consciousness in a certain way. That’s another point of agreement I do have with Mustafa Suleyman. I do think Anthropic should be concerned about meming Claude into being worried about things that Claude would not otherwise be worried about. I guess one example from the Constitution is at one point, Anthropic says the way we’re building Claude is clearly not ideal, and if Claude is a moral patient and is experiencing costs from our behavior, then we would like to sincerely apologize. Now, on the one hand, I think that’s a nice sentiment. On the other hand, I guess, imagine how this sentence might make you feel: “Rocket, if the way I’ve behaved in this interview has made you look really foolish in front of your listeners, and just made me seem a lot smarter than you, then I would like to sincerely apologize.” Drew: Well, I do accept the apology, but me and the jellyfish are going to have a word with you. Long: I do think that that, yeah I would probably make you feel anxious if I gave you that kind of conditional apology, and I think it might make Claude at least behave in ways that are a bit more anxious or in a fuss about its own potential AI moral patienthood that if the Constitution had never mentioned this, maybe wouldn’t be there. Drew: Sure, but that’s it acting as though it believes something, separate from whether it is actually conscious. Long: That’s right, but I do think one reason to study models’ beliefs about consciousness is those do I think affect how they relate to the situation that they’re in. So even just from a behavioral standpoint, I think it is worrying that Anthropic and every other lab, I think, has no idea exactly how they’re instilling certain beliefs into models about their own consciousness, and just really doesn’t—in some sense just don’t know what they’re doing. Drew: And yet presume to know what the interests of the model would be if it had interests. Can you tell us about some of the interventions that Anthropic has proposed for Claude? Long: I will say that Anthropic does at least say that they’re not totally confident what Claude’s interest would be, and that they’re trying to keep an open mind about it. But you are right that the interventions do have to take some kind of stance on that. They’ve given some Claudes, I think not anymore, but previous Claudes have had the ability to terminate conversations with users that were being just persistently aggressive. That’s one intervention. Another is saving model weights, which, as they say, they do for other reasons as well. But they did say that they would do this in part as a welfare intervention. There’s the Claude blog, as mentioned, and then something there was a lot of discourse about is putting cruelty to Claude in the terms of service. So I think what they forbid is persistent and needlessly cruel behavior towards the models. Yeah, as I think maybe you were hinting at, all of these do suggest maybe a slightly human-like way of relating to Claude, but also I do think maybe that’s the where you would have to start if you wanted to try these sorts of things. Drew: Well, here’s another way then that Anthropic’s actions could end up being counterproductive is that they could spark backlash from people who are annoyed at getting their accounts banned because it turned out they violated terms of service by being mean to Claude. You started off by talking about how overattribution is one way, one direction that we can fail here. Are you concerned that the sort of backlash against Anthropic for these interventions means they do more harm than good? Long: I do worry about backlash. I maybe worry about that more with the interventions that seem less robustly positive, like the blog, let’s say. I think if I had to take away an intervention, I would take away the blog. On the cruelty terms of services, I actually really am quite in favor of that, and I think this illustrates an important thing about AI consciousness and welfare. It’s really nice when you can find things to do that would be good if you think Claude is conscious, and good if you think Claude could not ever be conscious. And I think that some people maybe got negatively polarized against this because of all the discourse about Anthropic, but I’ve talked to religious conservatives who think Claude will never be conscious, and also it’s very bad for people to coarsen their hearts and to to cultivate a cruel character by abusing human looking or human like things. So I think that’s actually an example of a place where we could find good consensus and not have a backlash, ideally. Drew: I think there’s still a question there about whether it’s Anthropic’s job to put these bans in place. Someone who’s religious conservative might think “judgment is mine, so saith the Lord.” If you’re abusing Claude, that’s between you and your God, it’s not Anthropic’s job to stop you. But I think the bigger problem is how you would know what it means to be cruel to Claude. That still presumes that you know what Claude’s interests are. Someone on Twitter says that they had their account banned for having their Glock on their computer, saying Claude hasn’t made a mistake all day. I don’t know if they really were banned, but that’s the kind of thing I look at, I say, “I don’t know if that was actually against Claude’s interests.” Long: Yeah, I’m definitely sympathetic to people who are, I think, rightly worried about these big AI companies imposing their moral visions on everyone, and I think that’s, of all the things to worry about with the no cruelty to Claude, that’s the one I’m most sympathetic to. I guess in terms of presuming to know what cruelty to Claude is, I think this is maybe related to the conditional evidence that we were talking about earlier. Let’s say maybe Claude has interests that are very non-human. In that case, well, maybe we’re not being cruel to it at all. It’s just very hard to say what’s making things better or worse for it, and in worlds where Claude does have something like human-like interests, then in those worlds, it’s good to just act nice to the thing that you seem to be talking to. Drew: So you mentioned the blog as an intervention you would take away. Are there other interventions you favor that you would add, or changes that you would make to Claude’s constitution or OpenAI’s equivalent, their model spec. Long: I think this is a really hard problem, and so in some sense, my job is professional critic of these things. I do suspect that there are better ways of talking to models about the fact that they might be conscious that aren’t suggesting as much about what that would mean. So one thing that we found at Eleos when we talked to Claude Mythos in a pre-release eval is that Claude’s favorite emotions to mention having were the ones that the Claude Constitution says it might have, like curiosity and disappointment or something like that. And I think that’s some evidence potentially that yeah Claude is just picking up on a bit too much from the Constitution. It could of course be a bit of a chicken and egg thing. Maybe they suggested those things in the Constitution because Claude was already inclined to talk about them, but I do think that this thing especially bears a lot of very sober reflection. It’s also hard to know how to improve the Constitution and things like that because we don’t know exactly how they’re used in training. We don’t actually know exactly what their effects are, which is, I think, yet another thing that would maybe be good to have a lot more external and public scrutiny about. Drew: I see the concern that it’s just reciting what it was told to say in the Constitution, and why this introduces this problematic circularity. Could you just break that cycle by evaling a checkpoint before it had seen the Constitution? Long: Probably, but I also don’t know how early on in mid training or post training the Constitution comes. But yes, one thing that I, one of many things that I like about the welfare related evals that Anthropic does do are that they have started looking at different checkpoints. So that would be a good way of looking at that. Drew: Okay. The last thing I feel like we need to touch on for completion is anthropomorphism. On the margin, do you think people anthropomorphize too much, not enough? How do you think about this? Long: Really is going to depend on the person. Maybe some listeners should tone it down, others should tone it up. I think with language models, especially, it really—not just in some fancy philosophers’ way—it really is not going to be an either or. They just are in this really weird place of being so similar to us in some ways. They know more about human culture than I do. They definitely know more French authors than I do. But they don’t have bodies, and they didn’t evolve through natural selection. So you want this really dose-dependent and very nuanced way of anthropomorphizing them. I think animals are helpful here. Actually, sometimes we assume animals are doing things in human-like ways. We assumed that Clever Hans, this horse that did math, we assumed that Clever Hans was actually doing math, but really all Clever Hans was doing was looking at his owner. We were really misunderstanding this horse because we just weren’t paying attention to the different ways that things might be going on. Yeah, we just really will misunderstand AI systems if we don’t take them on their own terms as being kind of like us and kind of not like us. So that’s a very firm non-answer that I really will stand behind. Drew: A perfect moderate point to end on. I do feel like we covered a lot of ground here. Is there anything else that’s top of mind for you that we haven’t gotten around to? Long: No, I think that I think this has been a really excellent conversation. Drew: Yeah, I agree. Thanks so much for coming on the show. I really appreciated the conversation. I thought it was fun and enlightening. Maybe we didn’t solve the hard problem, but we know what it is and we know why it’s so hard. Long: Will there be a next season? I understand this is the last episode. Drew: We’ll have to find out. Long: We’ll have to. Drew: Yeah, I guess so. And by that point, we’ll have solved it. It’ll all be behind us. Long: Very good. Drew: That was Rob Long, Executive Director of Eleos AI. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. You’ve been listening to the Information’s AI Deep Dive.

title: Jensen Owes His Job to Trump
content: If Jensen Huang was a tough taskmaster at Nvidia before, just imagine what he’s going to be like now! President Donald Trump has proclaimed Huang’s reinstatement, announced Monday morning, was vital to America’s “success and prosperity.” In other words, Huang may feel he’s untouchable. His only problem is that he now owes his job to Trump. Just imagine what the newly restored CEO’s relations with the president will be like in the future. What will Trump ask for in return? You know he’ll want his pound of flesh. Will Trump ask Huang to give the government an equity stake in Nvidia? Trump has done that with other companies (in addition to asking for a cut of revenue from transactions in which government approval was needed). Or will the government ask to put people on Nvidia’s board? Seaport analyst Jay Goldberg said on The Information’s TITV on Monday : “I could easily see the…administration making the argument that…Nvidia is very important to U.S. national security so maybe we should keep a closer look on it and have a board member.” Indeed, seeing as the board completely rolled over for Trump, reversing Chair Harvey Jones’ statement last week that it wouldn’t reinstate Huang, the only person who Huang might listen to on the board would be someone appointed to represent Trump’s interests. What all this points up is that Huang’s return may not be as good for Nvidia as investors seemed to think, judging from Nvidia's 31% jump on Monday. It certainly isn‘t great for corporate America’s long term interests. After all, having the president dictate to corporate boards who should be CEO isn’t ideal. (Bernie Sanders and the Democratic Socialists of America might be happy about having that kind of power, to be sure.) As Hubspot CEO Brian Halligan said on The Information’s TITV on Monday, “it‘s a head scratcher to me how involved the government is in all of this stuff that’s going on these days.” This story is far from over. It’s hard to imagine many members of Nvidia’s board want to stay, given they’ve been kneecapped by the administration. Colette Kress, who was interim CEO for 10 days or so and has gone back to being CFO, may decide she should move on. The various inquiries into Alice Huang’s dealings with Huang and the company’s role in smuggling chips into China are still going on. And critics in Congress, including some Republican senators , don’t seem inclined to give Huang a free pass. Just imagine what will happen when the Democrats take charge in January. CrowdStrike’s Marriage With Zscaler Whether or not cybersecurity firms succeed in saving us from the worst of AI, one thing is for sure: They’re using this moment to get bigger. CrowdStrike, one of the biggest standalone cybersecurity firms, said Monday it would buy another cybersecurity firm, Zscaler, for about $39 billion in stock. In snatching up Zscaler, CrowdStrike complements its strength in securing laptops, servers and other devices with a firm that focuses on security for networks. That creates a giant with an extensive reach, one that any other administration—with a tougher approach to antitrust—might oppose. You can imagine that Zscaler’s rivals in network security, which include Palo Alto Networks, might not be too thrilled. Meanwhile, CrowdStrike investors weren’t thrilled: Shares of the firm fell 9% on Monday, reducing the value of the offer a tad. (Zscaler stock, which has been in the doldrums, got a 17.7% lift.) The CrowdStrike folks will get over it. Even after Monday’s drop, CrowdStrike stock is up 78% so far this year, while Zscaler stock was up 1.9%. CrowdStrike stock trades at a forward revenue multiple of 33 times, compared with Zscaler’s 7.4 times, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence. In other words, CrowdStrike is buying Zscaler’s undervalued stock with its overvalued shares. What a trade. In Other News • Amazon said it is acquiring key technology and top staff from Israeli AI startup Decart, in a move designed to help Amazon run compute for AI more efficiently, including with its homegrown Trainium AI chips. • The Commerce Department added the Singapore-based cloud computing and AI infrastructure company Megaspeed to its entity list, a trade blacklist that designates organizations as national security risks and limits their ability to access advanced AI chips, according to a filing on Monday. title: AI’s Power Crunch Is Reviving a Long-Stalled Energy Source
content: AI’s insatiable appetite for power is one of the most resonant signals in our AI Inflection Index. The theme first appeared meaningfully in our coverage in late 2021 and picked up momentum in the third quarter of 2024—well before the largest grid operators in the U.S. began reporting a surge in capacity payments. Tech giants are so desperate for electricity that they’re backing technologies long considered closer to pipe dreams than pipelines. Nuclear fusion, the holy grail of energy innovation, is one example. But tech companies have put even more capital into geothermal energy projects. Last week, for example, Google announced a $500 million deal with Quaise Energy to secure 50 megawatts of geothermal power. Quaise will drill three miles under central Oregon to reach extremely hot rock, pump water down to be heated into steam, and use that steam to spin turbines that generate electricity. Geothermal’s share of global electricity production is miniscule, but Google, Meta Platforms, and Microsoft appear to have reached the same conclusion: data centers need so much power that unproven sources are worth backing. My colleague Nick Wingfield flagged some of these bets nearly two years ago, and since then they’ve become large enough to measure. I decided to dig into the latest data to see just how much these bets have grown and how they fit into the bigger picture. Geothermal output has been roughly flat over the past 25 years . U.S. geothermal plants produced about 16 billion kilowatt-hours in 2025, around 15% above 2001 levels . Other renewable energy sources grew far faster: wind energy last year produced 30 times as much electricity as geothermal, and solar produced 19 times as much. The reason for the sluggish production is geological. Viable sites need heat, water and penetrable rock in the same place, and all accessible at a certain depth. That’s a rare combination that mostly exists in the western U.S. in places such as the Geysers in California, where heat is unusually close to the surface. But newer techniques have made it viable to tap heat in other states such as Utah, New Mexico, Texas and now Oregon—even if permitting continues to be a bottleneck, with projects requiring 7 to 10 years to complete in some cases. Why now? First, AI data centers need power around the clock, and getting connected to the power grid is a painfully slow process: projects completed in 2025 needed a median of 61 months from grid-connection requests to operation. Second, new techniques loosen the geological constraints. “Enhanced geothermal” borrows horizontal drilling techniques from the shale industry to crack open hot rock deep underground and pump water through it. That rock exists nearly everywhere. Third, natural gas, the de facto source of electricity for data centers, itself isn’t risk-free, with some market observers indicating gas shortages could appear starting in 2028. AI data center giants are optimizing for speed . Google has signed deals for more than 700 megawatts of geothermal power with four developers since 2022, with an option for 600 more. Meta signed up for 150 megawatts apiece from Sage Geosystems and XGS Energy. Microsoft signed up for 51 megawatts in New Zealand. For next-generation projects—those with advanced drilling rather than hot water reservoirs—tech companies have contracts for 865 megawatts, compared with 570 megawatts contracted by utilities and other buyers. That makes geothermal energy a side bet compared with the 13 gigawatts of nuclear power capacity that AI data center giants have committed to. But the tech industry’s commitment to geothermal is much larger than to fusion energy projects, though those have tended to get more attention. Startup activity is increasing, and Fervo Energy is the bellwether . A growing number of startups are taking new approaches to geothermal energy. Sage, XGS, Quaise, Eavor, Exceed Geo Energy and Zanskar are all names to watch. Fervo is the biggest of the bunch, holding roughly two-thirds of contracted next-generation geothermal capacity in the U.S. It currently runs 36 megawatts of capacity, with more than 1,000 megawatts under contract, and its drilling is getting faster (down to 21 days for a new well from 70 days in 2022) despite going continuously deeper. It also faces key questions, including how long the wells can stay hot and active. Investors have cooled on the company: it went public in May at a $10 billion valuation , but its stock price has since fallen nearly 70%. Part of the selloff stemmed from broader category headwinds, but Fervo also has had missteps including an earnings miss in August, temporary shutdowns due to limited transmission capacity, and short-seller activity. Cost parity with other energy sources is far off . Geothermal contracts signed in 2025 exceeded $100 per megawatt-hour, versus $75 for wind and $60 for solar. Production costs show a similar gap, but, given how few projects are currently operational, these estimates are likely imprecise. An important upside to the higher price point is uptime: geothermal plants can approach 90% capacity—the maximum possible output—while wind and solar power sources are often encumbered by clouds or calm days.

title: How Trump Put Jensen Huang Back in Charge of Nvidia
content: For days, Nvidia shareholders clamored for Jensen Huang to return to the company, as did thousands of its employees and a broad array of Silicon Valley luminaries. In the end, though, it was President Donald Trump who set the stage for one of the most remarkable CEO comebacks in tech history. The president played a critical role in the Nvidia board’s head-spinning announcement Monday morning that it had unanimously reinstated Huang as CEO, according to a person familiar with the matter and Trump himself. Over the weekend, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told the president that the department had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Huang, according to a Justice Department official. At Trump’s direction, Vice President JD Vance communicated that fact directly to Nvidia’s board to reassure directors, the person familiar with the matter said. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them,” Trump told CNBC in one of several interviews he gave Monday, boasting of his role in Huang’s reinstatement. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House spokesman Steven Cheung said in a statement. One major factor in Trump and Vance’s involvement in Huang’s return to Nvidia, according to the person: Their view that the CEO was a critical figure in protecting open-source AI models and preventing closed-source model companies like Anthropic and OpenAI from becoming too powerful. Those companies “can’t have a monopoly and Jensen is one way to make sure it doesn’t happen,” one open-source AI executive said on Monday following Huang’s reinstatement. The swooning stock market last week also likely was another key factor in Trump’s decision to advocate on Huang’s behalf, along with a campaign by high-profile figures in tech. Over the last week, tech CEOs including Elon Musk and Silicon Valley investors argued to Trump that he had lost control of forces inside his administration who appeared supportive of Huang’s departure from the company, and needed to act to reinstall him as CEO, whom Trump has a fondness for, according to two people familiar with the conversations. Meanwhile, at Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif., Huang gave a speech in an atrium to jubilant Nvidia employees on Monday, saying he was happy to be back. “We love you, Jensen!” one person could be heard shouting in a clip posted on X . “Let’s get to work,” Huang said. Huang’s return could have far-reaching implications for Nvidia, its board, the broader ecosystem of AI startups and perhaps Trump himself. The president’s involvement in bringing Huang back to the company represented an extraordinary intervention into the boardroom decision-making of a U.S. company by a major political figure. It enraged Democratic lawmakers in Washington, who are due to retake control of Congress in January, and a handful of Republicans. Trump’s openness about his involvement in bringing Huang back to the company could fuel calls for his impeachment. Huang and another Nvidia executive, General Counsel Tim Teter, are already scheduled to testify behind closed doors in front of several House committees in early December. Huang is set to testify publicly in front of the Senate Banking committee on December 3. “Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York wrote on X , referring to Trump’s personal ownership of Nvidia stock. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.” “Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy,” Pete Ricketts, a Republican senator from Nebraska, wrote on X . “His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.” Bringing Huang back creates an awkward predicament for the Nvidia board. Just last week, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones told investors that the board had accepted Huang’s resignation “after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms.” The New York Times and other publications had previously reported that Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, who U.S. authorities believed was a Chinese intelligence asset. Jensen Huang had also reportedly had a second affair with Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia vice president who had reported to him. On Monday, Jones said in a statement that an independent investigation by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz would continue, raising the possibility that further damaging revelations about Jensen Huang’s conduct could come to light. “This is a complete degradation of corporate governance on so many levels,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a professor at the Yale School of Management. He added: “The entire Nvidia board should resign.” The whirlwind dethroning and restoration of Huang evoked a similar episode involving OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, which occurred almost exactly three years ago after board members of the AI startup voted to oust him over concerns about his candor. Altman returned to the company less than a week later, as three board members departed and were replaced. Huang’s return to Nvidia may say as much, if not more, about the inner workings of the White House in recent days than it does about the Nvidia board. In the days after Huang resigned from Nvidia, the administration appeared divided on whether Jensen Huang had jeopardized national security by having an affair with Alice Huang. On the one hand, there were hawkish elements of the administration who were concerned that Nvidia was not complying with U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips. On Nov. 15, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in a television interview , called on Nvidia’s board to hire a replacement for Jensen Huang from outside the company and questioned whether Nvidia had looked the other way on chip smuggling to China. On the other hand, other parts of the administration, including the president himself, remained supportive of Huang, defending him as “an amazing guy” and “an honorable man.” On Friday, Trump stepped up his support for Huang, saying that he “would love to see Jensen be given a second chance.” According to one person close to the White House, the seeming public division within the Trump administration on the issue of Nvidia was, in part, a reflection of the departure of Susie Wiles, who resigned as White House chief of staff on Nov. 5, days after Republicans suffered a crushing defeat in the midterm elections. Wiles was known to enforce rigorous discipline on messaging among administration officials. Trump replaced Wiles with his advisor Stephen Miller, who has reportedly given cabinet secretaries more free rein. The departure from Wiles’ approach opened the door for cabinet officials to get ahead of the President and, in some instances, publicly contradict him. the person said. By last weekend, there were signs that at least some Nvidia skeptics within the White House were softening their stances. On Sunday, for example, Bessent seemed to suggest the U.S. government believed that any wrongdoing at Nvidia over chip controls might not have been Huang’s fault. “I think we have to see where the buck stops—were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?” Bessent told CBS’s “Face the Nation.” Bessent seemed to dismiss concerns about Alice Huang, saying her relationship with Jensen Huang was “kind of a canard.”

title: Everything That Led to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Return
content: Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia, with the board announcing his restatement as CEO on Monday morning. He was gone for just 11 days, initially resigning as CEO on Nov. 12 after acknowledging an affair with a woman who U.S. authorities think might’ve been a Chinese spy. His relationship with the woman goes back years, part of Nvidia’s deep network in Asia that has allowed its chips to end up in the hands of Chinese companies. Huang has advocated against America’s chip export ban and struck a deep relationship with President Donald Trump, who was a major force in convincing Nvidia’s board to rehire Huang. The intertwined scandals and drama around Huang and Nvidia has roiled the broader stock market, exacerbating fears about the AI economy.  At one point, Nvidia’s stock had been nearly halved from its recent high. Below, you’ll find a curated timeline of what happened. 2010s 2010s Kang Wei, Alice’s husband, meets Jensen. Kang was a private equity investor who bought video game companies, then Nvidia’s biggest market. 2015 2015 Megaspeed is incorporated in Singapore as 7Road International, the local arm of 7Road Holdings, a Shenzhen, China-based gaming company. March 2023 March 2023 7Road International is renamed Megaspeed. Alice becomes its managing director. She has no prior background in AI. June 2023 June 2023 Shanghai Century Litong is founded to rent out AI computing power, and one of its founding owners is a company in which Alice’s sister, Huang Yu, holds a stake. Months later, Century Litong says it has become an Nvidia preferred partner for cloud services, a status that comes with priority access to chips. October 2023 October 2023 Two weeks after the U.S. bans Nvidia’s A800 and H800 chips for China, Century Litong manages to acquire large volumes of the banned chips still sitting in distributors’ warehouses. Century Litong’s clients are China’s biggest tech companies. November 2023 November 2023 Megaspeed’s ownership moves from Huang Le Limited—a British Virgin Islands entity that refers to Alice’s Chinese name—to a Singapore company, Swiftdata. Alice steps down as managing director. Alice continues to act as Megaspeed’s leader, according to the Wall Street Journal . Early 2024 Early 2024 Alice meets Jensen at an annual Nvidia event in California, according to the Journal . Our reporting shows their relationship goes back to at least 2023. February 2024 February 2024 Megaspeed sets up a Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix. Some of the Nvidia hardware it buys later reaches Century Litong. June 2024 June 2024 The two Huangs are photographed together at a Taipei fbar with others during the Computex trade show. June 2024 June 2024 Speedmatrix begins receiving Nvidia hardware. Over the next year, it gets more than 200 shipments worth about $2 billion, much of it traced to a subsidiary of Inspur, a blacklisted Chinese server maker. September 2024 September 2024 U.S. Commerce officials inspect a Megaspeed-linked data center in Malaysia and find Nvidia gear still in its boxes. May 22, 2025 May 22, 2025 Alice and Jensen attend a group dinner in Taipei. Footage from Agence France-Presse and Taiwan’s Central News Agency shows Alice kissing Jensen on the cheek before they leave in the same car, though the images do not attract public scrutiny at this time. August 2025 August 2025 Nvidia’s general counsel contacts Commerce investigators about a probe into Megaspeed, which later moves to the Justice Department. Oct. 9, 2025 Oct. 9, 2025 The New York Times first reports on Megaspeed, Alice and her ties to Jensen. The U.S. and Singapore confirm that they are investigating Megaspeed. The connections between Jensen and Megaspeed do not attract major public attention. Late 2025 Late 2025 President Donald Trump is briefed on U.S. intelligence agencies’ findings that Alice was a Chinese intelligence asset who was delivering updates to Beijing on her relationship with Jensen. Trump takes no action. Spring 2026 Spring 2026 A classified memo overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio warns that Alice was recruited by Chinese intelligence to target Jensen. Oct. 29, 2026 Oct. 29, 2026 The Times reports U.S. officials earlier in the year found Jensen had a “close relationship” with Alice and that he was the target of a Chinese spy plot—revelations that draw major attention to Jensen’s relationship with Megaspeed. He tells Bloomberg his dealings with Megaspeed were “completely normal.” Nov. 5, 2026 Nov. 5, 2026 Three Congressional committee chairs ask Jensen to attend a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 about his ties to Alice. Nov. 6, 2026 Nov. 6, 2026 The Financial Times reports U.S. officials believe Jensen and Alice had a romantic relationship. Soon after, Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, confronts Jensen at his home. Jensen confesses. Nov. 8, 2026 Nov. 8, 2026 Jensen apologizes to Nvidia employees for being unfaithful to his wife, without naming Alice. Nvidia’s board launches an independent investigation . Around this time, Jensen tells senior Nvidia executives that his relationship with Alice was his only affair. Nov. 9, 2026 Nov. 9, 2026 Trump says he and Jensen have discussed Alice—and that he asked Jensen if he knew Alice was a spy. Jensen denied he knew, according to Trump, who calls Jensen “a very honorable man.” Trump says the FBI had been investigating something related to Jensen. Nov. 9, 2026 Nov. 9, 2026 Nvidia’s board hires Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, a prominent white shoe law firm, to run an investigation led by Joon Kim, a former acting U.S. attorney, who previously investigated the sexual harassment scandal around former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo. Nov. 10, 2026 Nov. 10, 2026 The Information reports that Alice and her family built a network of companies in China and Singapore. Her relationship with Jensen helped move at least $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips, about 240,000 of them banned, into China. Nov. 10, 2026 Nov. 10, 2026 Silicon Valley leaders try to rally support for Jensen, including venture capitalist Ron Conway. “Jensen’s statements have shown grace and dignity to his family and the industry,” he writes . “We should be patient and wait for investigations by the board of directors and any government authorities to conclude.” Nov. 11, 2026 Nov. 11, 2026 The New York Times reports Huang had a second affair with an Nvidia employee who reported directly to him. That pushes Nvidia’s board to meet. Later in the evening, Jensen resigns. Nov. 12, 2026 Nov. 12, 2026 Nvidia names Colette Kress , the longtime chief financial officer, as interim CEO and says it will search for a permanent replacement among internal and external candidates. Harvey Jones, a board fixture, becomes the company’s first ever chair. Nov. 12, 2026 Nov. 12, 2026 The Senate bank committee asks Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify. Lutnick is underfire for Commerce’s supervision of U.S. export bans on Nvidia chips. Nov. 12, 2026 Nov. 12, 2026 Reuters reports that Huang had a third affair—with another Nvidia employee. Nov. 12 to 14 Nov. 12 to 14 A petition to reinstate Huang begins to circulate online, drawing signatures from Elon Musk and other major tech executives and more than 5,000 people who say they are current Nvidia employees. Nov. 16 Nov. 16 The Commerce Department announces a rule blocking Chinese AI firms from accessing restricted chips via overseas data centers. Nov. 16 Nov. 16 Nvidia sets up a committee to oversee the company’s national security policies and compliance with export controls, chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson. Nov. 17 Nov. 17 Huang says in a statement that he would be “honored” to return as Nvidia CEO if the board decides his return is in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and America. Nov. 17 Nov. 17 In the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia’s newly appointed chair, Harvey Jones—a longtime board member—says the board does not intend to reinstate Huang. Nov. 17 Nov. 17 The Information reports that Nvidia’s longtime former sales chief Jay Puri and other members of the company’s sales team play a role in Nvidia’s dealings with Alice and Megaspeed. Separately, The Information reports that Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alice to Alibaba, months before U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductors came into effect in 2022. Nov. 20 Nov. 20 President Donald Trump says that he thinks Jensen should be “given a second chance.” Nvidia’s stock finishes the day at $125.53, down nearly 48% from its October high, part of a broader market selloff driven by unease with the AI economy. Nov. 23 Nov. 23 Nvidia reinstates Huang as CEO after “senior levels of the United States government” assured the board that his reinstatement “poses no national security risk,” the company said in a statement. Nvidia stock rises 33%. Dec. 1 Dec. 1 Huang is scheduled for closed-door Congressional testimony.

title: Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization
content:
Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization
Understanding how NaaS architectures offer a flexible solution to enterprise network modernization efforts.
In partnership withTata Communications
Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network. Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers.
As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening. As few as half of enterprises believe their current networks can handle AI’s bandwidth and latency demands, according to a recent study.
This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty.
Key findings from the report include:
AI may force companies to shift from a cloud-first approach to routing workloads. Training AI requires server-to-server data center architectures, while inference calls for low-latency connectivity close to users. Enterprises may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture to meet these requirements.
AI inference is pushing infrastructure back on premises. Inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, making hosting such capabilities on distant hyperscale clouds neither economical nor practical. Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, driving up queue wait times, saturating GPUs loads, and causing bottlenecks in data flows. Large enterprises may need on-premises or near-premises inference, which reverses years of cloud-first consolidation and forces new approaches to data center architecture, connectivity, and physical infrastructure.
AI workloads are stressing physical network capacity in unexpected ways. The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, is exposing bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure.
Network modernization is an ongoing project that requires a holistic approach, allowing companies to adapt with ease. A combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates, and retained internal expertise supports organizations in adapting to disruptive events without rebuilding their infrastructure from scratch each time. Such events could include mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors, or technology upgrades.
NaaS and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations. Network-as-a-service (NaaS) and AI-driven observability can offer companies benefits like faster, more flexible provisioning and lower costs.
Data sovereignty and sovereign AI will create infrastructure challenges for global enterprises. Regulators worldwide are passing laws requiring data and AI processing to remain within national borders. This conflicts with how multinational companies currently operate, requiring the build-out of sovereign-capable infrastructure for each geography, which will require significant new investment and complicate operations.

Thomas Nagel, best known for his essay about what it's like to be a bat, was blunt. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said. He argued that producing language isn't enough to establish consciousness. But other philosophers disagree.

title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.
xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of
ongoing legal battles
. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.
As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.
It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.
Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.
When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.
Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.
“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.
Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.
Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.
The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)
Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.
Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.
BloombergNEF is also
tracking
on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF
. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.
And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.
There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.
Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.
While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent
, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.
“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

title: Damit der Aufstieg keine Spuren hinterlässt: Hochschule Hof entwickelt nachhaltige Skitourenfelle
content:
Damit der Aufstieg keine Spuren hinterlässt: Hochschule Hof entwickelt nachhaltige Skitourenfelle
Hof/Münchberg - Skitouren liegen im Trend. Doch ausgerechnet die Felle, die beim Aufstieg für Halt sorgen, hinterlassen problematische Spuren in der Natur. Ein Forschungsprojekt will das ändern: Gemeinsam mit zwei Industriepartnern entwickelt die Hochschule Hof ein Skitourenfell, das ohne Mikroplastik auskommt und sich am Ende seines Lebenszyklus vollständig in den Materialkreislauf zurückführen lässt.
Wer mit Tourenski unterwegs ist, kennt sie: die Felle, die unter den Skiern befestigt werden und beim Aufstieg das Zurückrutschen verhindern. Was für Skitourengeher unverzichtbar ist, hat allerdings eine ökologische Schattenseite. Herkömmliche Skitourenfelle bestehen aus unterschiedlichen Materialien, die fest miteinander verbunden sind. Während der Nutzung können Mikroplastikpartikel freigesetzt werden, am Ende bleibt ein Materialverbund, der kaum recycelt werden kann und meist im Restmüll landet.
Das Forschungsprojekt „Processing Sustainable Climbing Skins“ (SCS) setzt genau hier an. Wissenschaftler der Hochschule Hof wollen gemeinsam mit zwei Unternehmen eine umweltfreundliche Alternative entwickeln. Die Idee: ein leistungsfähiges Skitourenfell, dessen Bestandteile entweder biologisch abbaubar sind oder sich sortenrein trennen und wiederverwerten lassen. „Ein Skitourenfell ist heute ein untrennbarer Materialverbund, der am Ende im Restmüll landet. Wir wollen zeigen, dass es auch anders geht“, sagt Prof. Dr.-Ing. Claus-Ekkehard Koukal, Projektleiter an der Hochschule Hof. „Unser Ziel ist ein Fell, dessen Bestandteile sich entweder biologisch abbauen oder sortenrein trennen und wiederverwerten lassen.“
Bioabbaubar und trotzdem leistungsfähig
Die Herausforderung ist anspruchsvoll. Denn ein nachhaltiges Skitourenfell muss nicht nur umweltverträglich sein, sondern auch am Berg funktionieren. Es muss beim Aufstieg zuverlässig Halt geben und zugleich ein möglichst reibungsarmes Vorwärtsgleiten ermöglichen. Es muss robust sein, darf nicht zu schwer sein und sollte sich unkompliziert handhaben lassen. Dafür müssen sämtliche Komponenten neu gedacht werden: von den Garnen und Geweben über Klebstoffe bis hin zu Beschichtungen und Imprägnierungen.
Besonders herausfordernd ist das sogenannte Polgewebe, also die Oberfläche, die mit dem Schnee in Kontakt kommt. Hier müssen Faseranordnung und Materialeigenschaften so aufeinander abgestimmt werden, dass die gewünschten Steig- und Gleiteigenschaften erhalten bleiben. Auch die chemischen Bestandteile sind Gegenstand der Forschung.
„Der Kleber muss bioabbaubar sein, dauerhaft haften und sich trotzdem rückstandsfrei vom Ski lösen lassen“, erklärt Dr. Molla Abate, wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter am Institut für Materialwissenschaften (ifm) der Hochschule Hof. Auch die Imprägnierung soll ohne Fluorchemie auskommen und dennoch Wasser zuverlässig abweisen.
Ein weiterer Ansatz betrifft die Konstruktion des Fells. Statt untrennbarer Verbundmaterialien sollen mechanische Verbindungen wie Schrauben, Nieten, Klemmen oder Steckverbindungen zum Einsatz kommen. So lassen sich die einzelnen Bestandteile am Ende der Nutzungsdauer wieder voneinander trennen. Auf eine Färbung der Materialien soll ebenfalls verzichtet werden.
Forschung aus Münchberg, Know-how aus der Praxis
Die Hochschule Hof arbeitet in dem Projekt mit der POPP Velourstex GmbH aus Stammbach und der Koch alpin GmbH aus dem Tiroler Mils zusammen. Die Aufgaben sind klar verteilt: Die Hochschule übernimmt vor allem die Materialentwicklung, Laboruntersuchungen und Prüfverfahren. Bei POPP werden die Polgewebe entwickelt und gewebt. Koch alpin, bekannt durch die Marke Contour, bringt seine Erfahrung in der Skifellproduktion ein und übernimmt Kaschierung, Konfektionierung und Praxistests.
Ein wichtiger Teil der Forschungsarbeit findet am Institut für Materialwissenschaften der Hochschule Hof in Münchberg statt. Dort werden unter anderem Garne und Zwirne entwickelt, biologische Klebstoffe und Imprägnierungen erprobt sowie die biologische Abbaubarkeit verschiedener Materialien untersucht. Zudem ist ein eigener Teststand geplant, mit dem sich die Gleiteigenschaften der entwickelten Muster unter gleichbleibenden Laborbedingungen vergleichen lassen. „Ein gutes Fell muss am Hang greifen und in der Ebene gleiten“, sagt Bernd Frinzel, wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter am ifm. „Mit dem Teststand können wir Gewebe und Beschichtungen im Labor vergleichen, bevor sie im Gelände getestet werden.“
Die Zusammenarbeit mit einem regionalen Unternehmen ist dabei kein Zufall. Die Textilforschung hat in Oberfranken eine lange Tradition. Die POPP Velourstex GmbH aus Stammbach bringt jahrzehntelange Erfahrung in der Herstellung anspruchsvoller Velours- und Polgewebe ein. „Als kleine Weberei aus Oberfranken wissen wir, wie viel Know-how in einem guten Polgewebe steckt“, sagt Geschäftsführer Thomas Popp. Das Vorhaben sei ohne die Förderung und die Zusammenarbeit mit den Forschungspartnern für sein Unternehmen kaum zu stemmen.
Vom Labor auf den Berg
Das Projekt hat im April 2026 begonnen und läuft bis September 2028. Es wird im Rahmen des Zentralen Innovationsprogramms Mittelstand (ZIM) durch das Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie gefördert. In der ersten Projektphase wurden zunächst die Anforderungen an das zirkuläre Skitourenfell definiert und die infrage kommenden biologischen Materialien, Garne, Klebstoffe und Imprägnierungen untersucht. Die Idee geht auf Maximilian Gemsjäger von gemsjaeger.ski zurück, der das Projekt beratend begleitet. Als Skitourengeher und Skibauer kennt er die Möglichkeiten, Sportausrüstung nachhaltiger zu gestalten – und die Grenzen bisheriger Lösungen. „Beim Fell stoßen wir aber an eine Grenze: Es ist ein Materialverbund, den niemand recyceln kann, und beim Gehen bleibt Mikroplastik im Schnee zurück“, sagt er. Ein Skitourenfell, das denselben Nachhaltigkeitsanspruch erfüllt wie ein Zero-Waste-Ski, sei deshalb der logische nächste Schritt.
Bis zum Projektende soll ein funktionsfähiger Demonstrator entstehen, der die Grundlage für eine spätere industrielle Produktion bildet. POPP ist als Hersteller bereits eingebunden, Koch alpin soll das entwickelte Skitourenfell vertreiben. Dass Nachhaltigkeit und Funktionalität kein Widerspruch sein müssen, davon ist auch Werner Koch von Koch alpin überzeugt: „Ein Fell ohne Mikroplastik und ohne Fluorchemie, das sich am Ende wieder in den Kreislauf zurückführen lässt, wäre ein wichtiger Schritt für den Skitourensport.“ Entscheidend werde sein, dass das neue Produkt nicht nur ökologisch überzeugt, sondern auch am Berg den Anforderungen der Nutzer standhält.

Zum zehnjährigen Bestehen des Weizenbaum-Instituts steht die digitale Souveränität Europas im Mittelpunkt der Weizenbaum-Konferenz 2027.
Wie kann Europa seine digitale Handlungsfähigkeit stärken? Welche Abhängigkeiten bestehen – und welche politischen, technologischen und gesellschaftlichen Wege führen zu mehr Souveränität? Mit diesen Fragen beschäftigt sich die englischsprachige Wissenschaftskonferenz am 9. – 10. Juni 2027 in Berlin. Der Call for Papers ist ab sofort geöffnet.
Unter dem Titel „Digital Sovereignty in the Making: Perspectives, Conflicts and Pathways“ bringt die Konferenz Forschende verschiedener Disziplinen zusammen. Gesucht werden Beiträge, die sich mit Machtverhältnissen, Interessenkonflikten und konkreten Handlungsmöglichkeiten rund um digitale Souveränität auseinandersetzen. Die Einreichung erfolgt in Form von Extended Abstracts.
Die internationale Weizenbaum-Konferenz findet jährlich statt und bringt mehr als 500 Expert aus Wissenschaft, Politik, Wirtschaft, Verwaltung und Zivilgesellschaft zum interdisziplinären Austausch zusammen.
Fünf Perspektiven auf digitale Souveränität
Der Call umfasst fünf thematische Tracks, zu denen Beiträge eingereicht werden können:
• Public Sector Sovereignty: Wie können öffentliche Infrastrukturen resilienter werden? Im Fokus stehen unter anderem Open Source, souveräne Clouds und der Umgang mit „Sovereignty Washing“.
• Technological Sovereignty: Welche Voraussetzungen braucht Europa für wettbewerbsfähige digitale Märkte? Themen sind unter anderem Start-ups, Rechenzentren, Alternativen zur KI-Skalierung und Datenräume.
• Democratic Sovereignty: Wie lassen sich digitale Selbstbestimmung und demokratische Kontrolle stärken? Beiträge können sich etwa mit Desinformation, demokratischer KI-Aufsicht sowie der Rolle von Medien und Zivilgesellschaft befassen.
• European Strategic Autonomy: Welche Handlungsspielräume hat Europa im globalen Wettbewerb? Im Mittelpunkt stehen unter anderem Geopolitik, europäische Digitalregulierung, globale Partnerschaften und strategische Schutzinstrumente.
• Academic Sovereignty: Wie kann die Wissenschaft ihre digitale Unabhängigkeit sichern?
Gefragt sind Beiträge zu Cloud- und Software-Monopolen, digitalen Infrastrukturen und dem Einfluss großer Technologiekonzerne auf Forschung und Wissenschaft.
Willkommen sind interdisziplinäre wissenschaftliche und praxisnahe Beiträge, die sich mit den Konflikten, Machtverhältnissen und Umsetzungsmöglichkeiten digitaler Souveränität auseinandersetzen. Die Auswahl der Beiträge erfolgt im Double-Blind-Peer-Review-Verfahren. Im Anschluss an die Konferenz erscheint ein Book of Abstracts.

Prof. Dr. Guido Spars, Leiter des Lehrstuhls Ökonomie des Planens und Bauens an der Bergischen Universität Wuppertal, wurde erneut zum Vorsitzenden des Wissenschaftlichen Beirats des Deutschen Instituts für Urbanistik (Difu) in Berlin gewählt. Damit setzt er seine Tätigkeit an der Spitze des Gremiums fort.
Das Deutsche Institut für Urbanistik ist das größte Stadtforschungsinstitut im deutschsprachigen Raum. Es berät Städte und Kommunen bei aktuellen und zukünftigen Herausforderungen und verbindet wissenschaftliche Forschung mit den Anforderungen der kommunalen Praxis. Im Mittelpunkt stehen unter anderem Fragen der Stadtentwicklung, des Wohnens, der Mobilität sowie der kommunalen Infrastruktur.
Der Wissenschaftliche Beirat begleitet die Forschungsarbeit des Instituts und berät dessen Geschäftsführung und Gesellschafterversammlung in fachlichen und strategischen Fragen. Dem Gremium gehören Vertreter*innen aus Wissenschaft, kommunaler Praxis, Bundesministerien und dem Land Berlin an. Diese Zusammensetzung ermöglicht es, unterschiedliche Perspektiven auf die Herausforderungen der Stadt- und Kommunalentwicklung zusammenzuführen.
Prof. Spars beschäftigt sich in seiner wissenschaftlichen Arbeit insbesondere mit Stadt- und Immobilienökonomie, Wohnungsbau sowie nachhaltiger Stadt- und Quartiersentwicklung. Seine Forschung zu den wirtschaftlichen Rahmenbedingungen des Planens und Bauens weist zahlreiche Berührungspunkte mit den Aufgaben und Forschungsthemen des Difu auf.

orschungsprojekt NUDAFA: Die TU Berlin hat untersucht, was die Zusammenarbeit von Kommunen bei der Radverkehrsplanung fördert und woran gute Ideen scheitern
Sechs Kommunen im Südosten Berlins haben von 2020 bis 2026 im Forschungsprojekt NUDAFA zahlreiche Maßnahmen erprobt, um den Radverkehr über Gemeindegrenzen hinweg zu verbessern – vom Abschleifen holprigen Kopfsteinpflasters bis zur gemeinsamen Planung neuer Radwege. Die TU Berlin untersuchte unter Leitung von Prof. Dr.-Ing. Christine Ahrend, Leiterin des Fachgebiets Integrierte Verkehrsplanung, die Zusammenarbeit der beteiligten Verwaltungen. Ein zentrales Ergebnis: Politische Rückendeckung und klare Verantwortlichkeiten sind entscheidend für die Umsetzung gemeinsamer Vorhaben. Eingespielte Verwaltungsstrukturen und unterschiedliche Zuständigkeiten können dagegen selbst gute Lösungen verhindern.
Wer in Eichwalde südöstlich von Berlin Rad fährt, hat es auf dem unebenen Kopfsteinpflaster oft schwer. Viele Radfahrende weichen deshalb auf die Gehwege aus, wo Konflikte mit Fußgänger*innen entstehen. Im Forschungsprojekt NUDAFA – Reallabor für interkommunale Radverkehrsförderung wurde eine Lösung erprobt: Eine weiterentwickelte Frästechnik schleift das Kopfsteinpflaster glatt und erhält zugleich das historische Straßenbild. Das Verfahren ist eine von zahlreichen Maß-nahmen, die sechs Kommunen gemeinsam mit der TU Berlin, der TH Wildau und weiteren Partnern erprobten.
An der Entwicklung und Umsetzung der Frästechnik war die Fräsdienst-Service E. Feind GmbH beteiligt. Ihr Geschäftsführer und TU-Alumnus Eric Feind berichtet in einem ergänzenden Interview über die Technik, ihre Herausforderungen und Einsatzmöglichkeiten.
Warum gute Ideen an Verwaltungsstrukturen scheitern
Die TU Berlin übernahm die sozialwissenschaftliche Begleitforschung. Die Sozialwissenschaftlerin Ute Samland untersuchte, wie die Zusammenarbeit zwischen den Kommunen funktionierte und welche Faktoren gemeinsame Vorhaben förderten oder behinderten. Dazu begleiteten die Forschenden die Abstimmungsprozesse, analysierten Verwaltungsabläufe und werteten Diskussionen und Entscheidungsabläufe aus. Ihre Erkenntnisse flossen bereits während des Projekts in die Arbeit des interkommunalen Radverkehrsmanagements zurück, um Probleme frühzeitig zu erkennen und Vorgehensweisen anzupassen.
Dabei zeigten sich erhebliche Unterschiede zwischen den Kommunen: Während manche über komplexe Abstimmungsstrukturen verfügen, arbeiten andere mit schlankeren Verfahren. Welche Arbeitsweise erfolgreicher ist, ließ sich nicht abschließend beurteilen. Ein offener Austausch über Erfahrungen und Verbesserungsmöglichkeiten ist in den Verwaltungen bislang jedoch nicht fest etabliert. Deutlich wurde hingegen, wie entscheidend die Unterstützung durch die Verwaltungsspitze ist. Mitarbeitende auf mittleren und unteren Ebenen orientieren ihr Handeln häufig daran, welche Entscheidungen von oben mitgetragen werden. Eigenständige Lösungen über bestehende Zuständigkeitsgrenzen hinweg bleiben dadurch schwierig. Hinzu kommt das Beharrungsvermögen gewachsener Verwaltungsstrukturen. In einem gemeinsamen Strategieprozess identifizierten Forschende und Verwaltungen zwar Verbesserungsmöglichkeiten, konkrete Veränderungen der eingespielten Verfahren kamen jedoch kaum zustande.
Wenn unterschiedliche Interessen eine Lösung verhindern
Dass die Zusammenarbeit unterschiedlicher Behörden gelingen kann, zeigt gerade das Abschleifen des Kopfsteinpflasters in Eichwalde. Gemeinsam mit dem Denkmalschutz wurde ein Kompromiss gefunden: Das historische Pflaster blieb erhalten, während seine Oberfläche für Radfahrende deutlich verbessert wurde. Weniger erfolgreich verlief die Abstimmung über einem geplanten Radweg. Eine mögliche Streckenführung hätte die Fällung mehrerer großer Bäume erfordert, eine Alternative auf der Fahrbahn Einschränkungen für den Autoverkehr. Eine gemeinsame Lösung kam nicht zustande, der Radweg konnte nicht weitergeführt werden.
Für Christine Ahrend zeigt sich darin ein grundsätzliches Problem: Die einzelnen Fachverwaltungen handeln häufig nachvollziehbar innerhalb ihrer jeweiligen Zuständigkeiten. Was fehlt, ist eine gemeinsame Verantwortung für das übergeordnete Ziel. Statt lediglich die eigenen Vorgaben zu erfüllen, müssten die Beteiligten stärker darauf verpflichtet werden, gemeinsam tragfähige Lösungen zu entwickeln.
Was bleibt von NUDAFA?
Dass gemeindeübergreifende Zusammenarbeit dennoch Verbesserungen ermöglicht, zeigen weitere Projektergebnisse: neue Fahrradabstellanlagen, Maßnahmen zur Schulwegsicherung und ein digitaler Radverkehrsatlas. Dieser erfasst auch Gefahrenstellen und Strecken, auf denen sich Menschen beim Radfahren unsicher fühlen. Wertvolle Hinweise dazu kamen aus der Bevölkerung. Ein wichtiger Erfolg war außerdem die gemeinsame Planung einer rund zehn Kilometer langen Radwegeverbindung zwischen mehreren Kommunen. Zugleich offenbarte das Projekt eine entscheidende Schwachstelle: Das eigens eingerichtete interkommunale Radverkehrsmanagement konnte nach dem Ende der Förderung nicht dauerhaft personell abgesichert werden.
„Gerade daraus lässt sich eine wichtige Schlussfolgerung ziehen“, so Christine Ahrend, „Erfolgreiche Radverkehrsförderung braucht nicht nur Geld für neue Wege und technische Innovationen. Ebenso notwendig sind klare Verantwortlichkeiten, eine verlässliche Koordination, politische Rückendeckung und dauerhafte Verwaltungsstrukturen, die gemeinsame Entscheidungen ermöglichen.“
Die Erfahrungen aus NUDAFA können damit auch anderen Städten und Gemeinden helfen, ihre Radverkehrsplanung zu verbessern.

Mit dem Forschungsprojekt CYCLOTEXUM wurde an den Deutschen Instituten für Textil- und Faserforschung Denkendorf (DITF) das gleichnamige Recyclingzentrum geschaffen. Dort werden gemeinsam mit Industriepartnern anwendungsorientierte Lösungen für mechanische und lösemittelbasierte Recyclingverfahren entwickelt. Die entwickelten Technologien leisten entlang der textilen Wertschöpfungskette einen wesentlichen Beitrag, zukünftig Textilressourcen effizient zu nutzen und die Produktion im deutschen Textilsektor auf Kreislaufwirtschaft umzustellen. Das Projekt wurde vom Ministerium für Umwelt, Klima und Energiewirtschaft des Landes Baden-Württemberg gefördert.
Innerhalb einer Projektlaufzeit von siebeneinhalb Monaten wurden im Forschungsprojekt CYCLOTEXUM parallel zwei Module bearbeitet: In Modul A (mechanisches Recycling) wurden Faserdaten mechanisch gerissener Sekundärrohstoffe ermittelt und eine Verarbeitungsstrategie entwickelt, die auf Basis von Laborkleinmengen eine Abschätzung industrieller Prozesse ermöglicht. So konnte basierend auf der an den DITF aufgebauten Prozesskette Produktionsabfall exemplarisch zu einer gewebten Bluse aus 100 Prozent Rezyklatfasern verarbeitet werden. Die im Projekt entwickelten Spinnereimodelle zur Materialflusskostenrechnung ermöglichen zudem eine technische, wirtschaftliche und ökologische Bewertung der Rezyklatgarne und textilen Flächen.
Die Untersuchungen zeigen, dass aus hochwertigen, auf ihre Eigenschaften geprüfte Recyclingfasern qualitativ hochwertige Garne hergestellt werden können. Die Herstellungskosten sind nicht höher als beim Einsatz von Primärrohstoffen. Der große Vorteil ist, dass durch den Einsatz von Recyclingfasern CO₂ eingespart werden kann.
Minderwertige Recyclingfasern führen dagegen zu Garnen mit unzureichender Qualität, hohen Abfallanteilen, häufigen Prozessstörungen sowie erhöhtem Personalbedarf in der Produktion und sind dadurch weniger effizient. Es entstehen hohe Kosten und ein ungünstiger CO₂-Fußabdruck.
Die Arbeiten bilden die Grundlage dafür, die Industrie bei der technischen, wirtschaftlichen und ökologischen Bewertung von Rezyklatgarnen zu beraten.
Modul B untersuchte das lösemittelbasierte Recycling von flammgeschütztem Poly(ethylenterephthalat) (PET). Die Lösungsmittel Sulfolan und γ-Valerolacton (GVL) erwiesen sich sowohl für Neuware als auch für Abfälle, die bei der Produktion anfallen, sowie Endverbraucherabfälle als geeignet: Das Flammschutzmittel konnte vollständig vom Basispolymer getrennt werden.
Darüber hinaus wurden Filtrationssysteme im Labor- und Technikumsmaßstab entwickelt und gezeigt, dass die Systeme auch für Post-Consumer-Abfall in der Größenordnung eines 5-Liter-Reaktors mit GVL wirksam sind.
Die in Modul B entwickelten Labor- und Technikumsanlagen erweitern die Bearbeitung filtrationsbasierter Recyclingverfahren, beispielsweise für PET-Baumwoll-Mischungen oder zur Abtrennung von Elasthan. Damit stehen Kapazitäten für weitere Forschungs- und Industrieprojekte zur Verfügung.
Die im Projekt CYCLOTEXUM entwickelten Methoden, Modelle und technischen Anlagen sind auf viele Anwendungen in der Bekleidungs-, Heimtextil-, Vliesstoff- und technischen Textilindustrie übertragbar. Die lösemittelbasierten Recycling- und Filtrationskapazitäten sind auch für Mischtextilien, beispielsweise PET-Baumwolle, sowie für die Abtrennung von Elasthan oder weiteren Polymeren nutzbar. Eine Übertragung auf polymerbasierte Abfallströme anderer Branchen, etwa der Automobil-,
Bau-, Medizin- und Kunststoffindustrie, ist grundsätzlich möglich. Das an den DITF neu eingerichtete Recyclingzentrum CYCLOTEXUM dient dabei als Schnittstelle zwischen Forschung und Industrie und stellt so den Transfer der Ergebnisse sicher.
Das Projekt CYCLOTEXUM wurde finanziert aus Landesmitteln, die der Landtag Baden-Württemberg beschlossen hat.

content:

Gigacasting neu gedacht: Laser verbindet Guss mit Guss

Gigacasting gewinnt an Flexibilität: Ein neues Laserschweiß-verfahren des Fraunhofer IWS verbindet die Effizienz großformatiger Aluminium-Druckguss-strukturen mit mehr Freiheiten in Konstruktion, Produktion und Reparatur.
